docs.title: MedEnroll834 Documentation
docs.text:
A Modern Distributed Data Platform for Growing Data — a healthcare X12 834 enrollment modernization prototype built on PySpark, Delta Lake, Databricks, Apache Airflow, and PostgreSQL.

Start with Chapter 0 — Healthcare Enrollment Primer if you're new to healthcare enrollment terminology, or jump straight to Chapter 1 — Project Overview for the technical scope.

docs.title: 00. Healthcare Enrollment Primer
docs.text: This chapter is for readers new to U.S. healthcare administration. It defines the terms, programs, and regulatory concepts used throughout this documentation — read it first if phrases like "834," "Medicaid managed care," or "HIPAA X12" aren't already familiar.

docs.title: What is an "834"?
docs.text:
834 is the name of a specific electronic document format — formally, the ANSI ASC X12 834 Benefit Enrollment and Maintenance transaction. Health insurers, employers, and government agencies use it to tell each other "this person is enrolling in (or changing, or ending) this health plan." It is one of dozens of numbered X12 transaction types used in U.S. healthcare administration; others include 837 (claims), 835 (payment/remittance), and 270/271 (eligibility inquiry/response). This project processes only 834 files.

An 834 file is not human-readable prose — it is a structured text format with fixed segment codes (ISA, GS, ST, HL, NM1, DTP, HD, ...), each carrying specific pieces of information (a name, a date, a plan code) in a fixed position. Chapter 12 covers exactly how this project parses that structure.

docs.title: Why "HIPAA X12"?
docs.text: HIPAA (the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996) is the U.S. federal law best known for patient-privacy rules, but it also mandates that health plans and providers use standardized electronic transaction formats — specifically, the X12 standard published by ASC X12 — for exchanges like enrollment, claims, and eligibility checks. "HIPAA X12 834" is shorthand for "the federally mandated standard enrollment transaction format." Using a non-standard, proprietary format for these exchanges is not legally permitted for covered entities, which is part of why every health plan ingests the same 834 structure regardless of which vendor built its systems.

docs.title: Who is enrolling in what? The core entities
docs.text:
Term Plain-language meaning Member A specific person covered by a health plan — could be the policyholder or one of their dependents. Subscriber The member who is the primary policyholder — the person whose employment, Medicaid eligibility, or marketplace application the coverage is based on. Dependent A member covered through a subscriber's policy — a spouse, child, or domestic partner, per the 834's relationship code. Employer group The organization (an employer, or a state Medicaid program) whose contract with the health plan covers a population of subscribers. Benefit plan The specific product a member is enrolled in (e.g. an HMO, a PPO, a specific metal tier) — determines what's covered and how. Enrollment The event of a member being added, changed, or termed on a benefit plan — the "transaction" an 834 file communicates.

These six concepts map directly onto this project's data model — see Chapter 1's conceptual model and Chapter 9's schema.

docs.title: Medicaid, Medicare, and the marketplace — who pays, and who's eligible
docs.text:
Program Who it's for Who runs it Medicaid Low-income individuals and families; eligibility rules vary by state Jointly funded by federal and state governments; administered by each state, often through contracted managed care organizations CHIP (Children's Health Insurance Program) Children in families who earn too much for Medicaid but can't afford private coverage Same federal/state structure as Medicaid, often administered alongside it Medicare People 65+, or younger people with certain disabilities Fully federal (via CMS — the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services) Medicare dual-eligible People who qualify for both Medicare and Medicaid Coordinated between federal Medicare and state Medicaid benefits ACA Marketplace (also "Affordable Care Act Marketplace" or "Exchange") Individuals/families buying private coverage directly, often with income-based federal subsidies Federal framework (HealthCare.gov or a state-run exchange); plans sold by private insurers Commercial/employer-sponsored Employees (and dependents) covered through an employer's group health plan Fully private, negotiated between employer and insurer

A managed care organization (MCO) is a private health plan that a state contracts with to administer Medicaid (and sometimes Medicare dual-eligible and Marketplace) benefits on the state's behalf — this is the kind of organization whose enrollment processing this project models (see Chapter 2).

docs.title: Why enrollment data is time-sensitive
docs.text: A member's coverage record has to be accurate and current before a pharmacy, doctor's office, or hospital can rely on it — a claim submitted for a service the plan doesn't yet show the member as covered for will be rejected or delayed, even if the member is, per the state or employer, actually enrolled. This is the real-world reason enrollment file processing speed ("Velocity" in the Three-V framing used throughout this documentation) matters operationally, not just as an abstract performance metric.

docs.title: Relationship codes used in this project
docs.text:
The 834's INS segment carries a numeric relationship code identifying how a dependent relates to their subscriber. This prototype's generator and validator use four of the most common codes:

Code Relationship 18 Self (the subscriber) 01 Spouse 03 Child 19 Domestic partner

docs.title: Terms you'll see throughout this documentation
docs.text:
Term Meaning EDI (Electronic Data Interchange) The general practice of exchanging structured business documents (like 834s) electronically between organizations, instead of paper/fax. Plan code / plan tier A short code identifying a specific benefit plan product (this project's synthetic data uses tiers like GOLD, SILVER, BRONZE, PLATINUM, HDHP, EPO, PPO, HMO). Coverage start/end date The date range a member's enrollment in a plan is effective — an open-ended (still-active) enrollment has no end date yet. Termination ("term") Ending a member's coverage on a plan, as opposed to adding or changing it. Group number An identifier for the employer group or state contract a subscriber's coverage is issued under. PHI / PII Protected Health Information / Personally Identifiable Information — the categories of sensitive data HIPAA and general privacy law protect. This project uses zero real PHI/PII; all data is synthetically generated (see Chapter 10).

With these fundamentals in place, Chapter 1 picks up with how this project's own pipeline is scoped and structured.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
MedEnroll834 is a modernization prototype for healthcare enrollment processing. It models a production-style pipeline for inbound HIPAA X12 834 transactions — the standard EDI format carriers and employers use to enroll, change, and terminate member benefit coverage.

The prototype demonstrates a faster, more observable, and more reliable operating model than the legacy file-handoff chain it replaces. It does not use production member data — all 834 files are synthetically generated (see Chapter 10).

docs.title: Objectives
docs.text:
• Handle high-volume enrollment files through distributed processing (PySpark on Databricks) instead of a single-machine batch job.
  • Preserve raw source data and track every transformation (Bronze → Silver → Gold medallion architecture with Delta Lake).
  • Serve both operational enrollment processing (PostgreSQL OLTP) and analytical reporting (Delta Lake star schema + Databricks SQL), explicitly kept as two separate consumption paths.
  • Demonstrate modern data-engineering practices — idempotent pipelines, data-quality quarantine, Airflow orchestration, CI/CD, and Infrastructure as Code — in a this project.

docs.title: Conceptual model
docs.text:
At a conceptual level, five business entities drive the whole system: a member belongs to a subscriber's policy, the subscriber is covered under an employer group's contract, that group offers one or more benefit plans, and every addition, change, or termination to a member's coverage is captured as an enrollment event. The pipeline's entire job is to take an inbound 834 file, resolve these five entities and the relationships between them, and make the result available two ways at once: as live, queryable records for operational use (a member's current plan, a subscriber's dependents) and as historical, aggregated records for analytical use (enrollment trends by plan, by group, by time period).

Rejected/invalid records enter a controlled remediation path (quarantine) rather than silently failing or corrupting downstream tables — see Chapter 16.

docs.title: Target workflow
docs.text:
1. Receive an 834 file from a (synthetic, in this POC) external source.
  2. Land the original file in object storage (S3-compatible blob storage in the POC, AWS S3 in the enterprise target).
  3. Parse, validate, and normalize member enrollment transactions with PySpark (EDI834Parser, SilverLayer).
  4. Apply plan-assignment business rules (GoldLayer).
  5. Load operational enrollment data into PostgreSQL (load_gold_to_oltp).
  6. Publish curated Delta tables (OLAP star schema) for analytics and dashboards (Databricks SQL + Genie).

Apache Airflow coordinates the end-to-end workflow (med834_e2e_pipeline DAG). Databricks provides scalable processing, Delta Lake storage, and SQL analytics.

docs.title: Design principles
docs.text:
• Idempotent and incremental — natural-key upserts (ON CONFLICT ... DO UPDATE) in the OLTP loader, overwrite/append semantics with mergeSchema in the Delta layers.
  • Invalid records are quarantined with actionable rejection reasons (validation_errors array column), not silently dropped.
  • Every run emits metrics, logs, and lineage signals — setup_logging, log_pipeline_start/log_pipeline_end, and run summaries returned from each layer ({"bronze_segments": ..., "silver_valid": ..., "gold_records": ...}).

docs.title: Success measures
docs.text:
The prototype targets the legacy system's velocity, volume, and variety constraints described in Chapter 2. A validated smoke-test run (1 synthetic file, 3 subscribers + 3 dependents) produced:

BRONZE     : segments_loaded = 83
SILVER     : total = 6, valid = 6, invalid = 0
GOLD       : records = 6
QUARANTINE : records = 0

See Chapter 34 for the full legacy vs. modern comparison and what is measured vs. what is a design target.

docs.title: Business drivers
docs.text:
Healthcare enrollment processing relies on timely, accurate HIPAA 834 transactions. The current (legacy) workflow uses a chain of specialized tools and scheduled jobs rather than a unified, distributed pipeline.

An inbound 834 file arrives in a designated folder. An EDI job converts the transaction into a proprietary format. An ECA job evaluates each member and assigns a plan. A Legacy Programs process generates a keyword file for the downstream CORE System. CORE Programs then loads the enrollment result.

The legacy implementation chains together Tidal scheduling, SSIS, DataStage, Legacy Programs, SCP file movement, Bash validations, and the CORE Programs load. Each handoff adds an operational dependency and a potential failure point — see Chapter 3 for the full flow diagram.

docs.title: Current constraint (observed)
docs.text: Enrollment processing jobs in the legacy system are observed to take approximately one hour end to end for a full daily batch file. Database locks and single-machine processing limit throughput. Investigating a failure across six-plus disparate tools can delay recovery significantly, since each tool keeps its own logs and none share a common run/lineage identifier.

docs.title: Volume — an industry-wide growth trend, not a one-time spike
docs.text: Total U.S. health insurance enrollment grew significantly through the COVID-19 pandemic years, reaching roughly 297 million covered individuals by late 2025, before entering a period of policy-driven contraction heading into 2026 — largely due to the "Great Unwinding" of continuous Medicaid eligibility and the expiration of pandemic-era ACA premium tax credits. Even accounting for that contraction, the underlying structural trend for managed care organizations has been sustained, multi-decade membership growth punctuated by sharp step-changes (pandemic enrollment surges, Medicaid expansion, new ACA Marketplace lines of business). A fixed-capacity, single-machine legacy pipeline has no way to absorb that kind of growth or a sudden policy-driven enrollment swing without a hard redesign — only horizontally scalable, distributed processing can expand capacity on demand rather than hitting a hard ceiling.

docs.title: Velocity
docs.text: Enrollment changes require prompt processing — a member's coverage often needs to be active before a claim is submitted. Long batch windows delay downstream availability and operational response.

docs.title: Variety
docs.text: 834 transactions contain varying member, employer, subscriber, group, and plan information — different relationship codes (self/spouse/child/domestic partner), different plan products (GOLD, SILVER, BRONZE, PLATINUM, HDHP, EPO, PPO, HMO in this prototype's validation rules — see DataFrameValidator.VALID_PLANS in src/medenroll834/quality/validator.py), and segments that may be mixed ~-terminated or newline-terminated within the same file (split_segments() in src/medenroll834/ingestion/bronze.py normalizes both). The pipeline must validate these differences without losing source traceability back to the raw segment.

docs.title: Business objective
docs.text: The prototype shows how a modern, distributed data platform can address all three constraints simultaneously: it improves throughput (parallel Spark execution vs. serial single-machine jobs), observability (structured logs + run summaries + Delta table lineage instead of six separate tool logs), recoverability (idempotent re-runs, quarantine instead of hard failure), and analytical access (an OLAP star schema and Databricks SQL/Genie that the legacy CORE System-only flow does not provide). It is also a practical modernization blueprint for presenting an architecture decision to stakeholders.

docs.title: 03. Legacy Architecture
docs.text:
Conceptual overview

This is an illustrative view of a traditional X12 834 enrollment processing workflow — file ingestion, format conversion, business-rule application, batch orchestration, validation, and integration with a downstream core administration system. It represents a generalized, educational architecture pattern commonly seen in healthcare enrollment processing and is not intended to reproduce any specific organization's production environment, internal job names, or proprietary workflow details.

docs.title: Existing platform
docs.text: The legacy process is a scheduled, file-based enrollment workflow. It moves data across specialized tools before the CORE System receives the final keyword file — there is no single distributed processing engine or shared data lake underneath it.

docs.title: Processing flow
docs.text:
1. A federal or external source places an 834 file in a monitored folder.
  2. An EDI job converts the 834 transaction into a proprietary format.
  3. An ECA job processes each member and assigns a benefit plan.
  4. A Legacy Programs process generates the keyword file.
  5. SCP and Linux jobs move files and run Bash validations.
  6. CORE Programs loads the keyword file into the CORE System core platform.

Tidal schedules and coordinates the jobs. SSIS and DataStage support loading and transformation activities elsewhere in the estate.

flowchart LR
    SRC["834 File(federal / external source)"] --> EDI["EDI Job(proprietary conversion)"]
    EDI --> ECA["ECA Job(plan assignment)"]
    ECA --> EXE["Legacy Programs Process(keyword file generation)"]
    EXE --> SCP["SCP + Bash(file movement & validation)"]
    SCP --> CORELOAD["CORE Programs Load"]
    CORELOAD --> CORESYS["CORE System(core administration platform)"]

    WLA["Tidal(workload automation / job scheduling)"] -.schedules.-> EDI
    WLA -.schedules.-> ECA
    WLA -.schedules.-> EXE
    WLA -.schedules.-> SCP
    WLA -.schedules.-> CORELOAD

    SSIS["SSIS / DataStage"] -.supports.-> EDI
    SSIS -.supports.-> ECA

docs.title: Operational limitations
docs.text:
• Sequential file handoffs. Each stage must complete and hand a file to the next tool; there is no parallelism within a stage.
  • Fragmented logging. Each tool maintains separate logs and operational controls — there is no common run ID connecting an EDI failure to its downstream ECA or CORE System load.
  • Database contention. Single-machine, serial processing against a shared database can create lock-related delays or failures under load.
  • Limited parallelism. All transformation work happens on one machine, so the observed ~1 hour processing-time constraint (see Chapter 2) cannot be improved without adding distributed compute.
  • Proprietary intermediate format. The EDI → proprietary conversion complicates reuse: the data cannot easily be queried, re-processed, or fed into an analytics stack without a custom reader.
  • Operational-only data shape. The data produced is optimized purely for the CORE System keyword-file load, not for broad analytics, historical reporting, or ad hoc BI/AI querying.

docs.title: Modernization boundary
docs.text: CORE System remains the downstream system of record in this prototype's conceptual framing. The modernization effort documented in this documentation focuses on ingestion, transformation, validation, and data delivery — replacing the EDI → ECA → Legacy Programs → SCP → CORE Programs Load chain with a distributed PySpark/Delta/Airflow pipeline (see Chapter 4) while keeping the downstream operational contract (an enrollment record reaching a core administration system) conceptually the same.

docs.title: Idea: Modern Distributed Data Platform for Growing Data
docs.text:
This proof of concept demonstrates how distributed processing can prepare a healthcare data platform for increasing data volume, velocity, and variety. X12 834 enrollment processing is the representative business module; the architecture is designed to be reusable across other business domains.

Note

"Enrollment" names the representative POC module, not the platform itself. The platform capability being demonstrated is distributed processing plus operational/analytical separation, applicable to any high-volume healthcare (or other) data domain.

docs.title: Three capabilities
docs.text: The architecture delivers three distinct, composable capabilities, in the order data actually flows through them. Keeping them conceptually separate is the core of the modernization story.

docs.title: Capability 1 — Distributed Processing
docs.text:
X12 834 → Landing (object storage) → Databricks / PySpark → Bronze → Silver → Gold

Purpose: Handle increasing Volume, Velocity, and Variety by parsing and validating EDI data as a distributed, replayable medallion pipeline rather than a monolithic nightly batch job.

docs.title: Capability 2 — Transactional Platform
docs.text:
Gold → PostgreSQL OLTP database → Operational applications

Purpose: Provide an operational relational store for application-facing reads/writes, decoupled from analytical query load.

docs.title: Capability 3 — Analytical Platform
docs.text:
Gold → Star Schema (Delta Lake) → Databricks SQL → BI/HTML Reports + Genie AI

Purpose: Separate analytical workloads from operational systems and provide governed data for BI and AI use cases, independent of the transactional (OLTP) store.

docs.title: Architecture layers
docs.text:
1. Ingestion — Synthetic / real X12 834 files land in object storage, then get staged into a Databricks Unity Catalog Volume (/Volumes/med834enrl/edi/landing/834) so serverless Databricks compute can read them.

2. Distributed processing (Databricks / PySpark) — Bronze: raw X12 segments, one row per segment, schema fixed but content untouched. Silver: validated, normalized member records with a validation_errors array and is_valid flag; invalid rows go to DQ / Quarantine. Gold: analytics-ready deduplicated enrollment records with derived fields (full_name, age_years).

3. Two downstream consumers of Gold — OLTP load: load_gold_to_oltp() upserts Gold rows into the PostgreSQL CORE/ENRL schemas for operational applications. OLAP star schema: the same Gold data is modeled into DIM_MEMBER, DIM_PLAN, DIM_GROUP, DIM_DATE, DIM_TRANSACTION_SOURCE, and FACT_ENROLLMENT for BI/dashboarding and AI/Genie natural-language analytics.

docs.title: 4. Analytical consumption — two modes
docs.text:
Both the HTML report and Genie are consumers of the governed analytical layer, not steps inside the pipeline's transformation logic.

Mode Flow Use case Traditional analytics Predefined SQL → HTML report Fixed KPIs, scheduled reporting AI analytics Natural language → SQL → result Ad hoc exploration via Genie

docs.title: 5. Orchestration — Airflow
docs.text: Airflow orchestrates the end-to-end workflow, including ingestion, Databricks processing, OLTP loading, reporting, and archival, with task dependencies, retries, and failure handling. Airflow sits above the pipeline as orchestration — it is not a data layer itself. The archive step runs with the default all_success trigger rule, wired directly to the core processing chain's own outputs, so files are only archived once Databricks and the OLTP load have actually succeeded; a separate quarantine_failed_files task (trigger_rule="one_failed") moves this run's files to a failed/ prefix instead if that chain fails. See Chapter 20.

docs.title: 6. POC vs. enterprise storage
docs.text:
For the proof of concept, S3-compatible blob storage and Databricks Unity Catalog Volumes provide the development storage path. In the target enterprise architecture, the landing/object-storage layer can be implemented using AWS S3 while retaining the same downstream Bronze-Silver-Gold, OLTP, OLAP, BI, and AI architecture — the interface is already implemented in src/medenroll834/s3/s3_utils.py alongside the POC's src/medenroll834/storage/blob_storage.py.

See also: End-to-End Execution and Docker / Local Development (includes the backout/rollback procedures).

docs.title: 05. Technology Decisions
docs.text: Every technology choice below is pinned in requirements.txt / pyproject.toml and actually exercised by the pipeline — this is not an aspirational stack list.

docs.title: Processing engine: PySpark 4.0+ / Delta Lake 4.0+
docs.text:
Why: Distributed DataFrame processing scales horizontally with data volume (the core "Volume" constraint from Chapter 2), and Delta Lake adds ACID transactions, schema evolution (mergeSchema), time travel, and Change Data Feed (delta.enableChangeDataFeed) on top of plain Parquet. The medallion layers (src/medenroll834/ingestion/{bronze,silver,gold}.py) write exclusively in Delta format.

Why Delta over plain Parquet: Parquet alone is already a columnar, compressed format — splitting data into column chunks means a query that only needs a few fields (e.g. plan_id, coverage_start_date) reads far less from disk than a row-oriented format would, and per-column min/max statistics let Spark skip whole files that can't match a filter. Delta Lake keeps that storage format but adds a transaction log on top of it: concurrent/retried writes (an Airflow retry re-running Bronze) can't corrupt or partially overwrite a table, mergeSchema lets a layer tolerate an added column without a manual migration, and delta.enableChangeDataFeed lets a future consumer read only the rows that changed since a given version instead of re-scanning the whole table (see Chapter 37 for where this is headed next).

docs.title: Orchestration: Apache Airflow 3.x (TaskFlow API, CeleryExecutor)
docs.text: Why: The core requirement here is production-grade orchestration — a task-dependency graph, automatic retries with backoff, and visibility into every run — delivered by a widely-adopted, actively maintained open-source project with a large operator/provider ecosystem (official Databricks and AWS provider packages, in this case) rather than a proprietary scheduler. The @dag/@task TaskFlow decorators (05_orchestration/airflow/01_dags/med834_e2e_pipeline.py) keep each stage as a typed Python function with explicit inputs/outputs, and the same DAG definition runs identically in this project's own Docker Compose stack or in a managed service (MWAA, Cloud Composer, Astronomer) with no code change — a proprietary enterprise scheduler would require a dedicated license and operator training, while Airflow's skill set and DAG code are directly portable.

docs.title: Compute platform: Databricks (Free/Serverless tier compatible)
docs.text: Why: Managed Spark clusters, Unity Catalog governance, and Databricks SQL warehouses in one workspace, with a SQL-callable WorkspaceClient SDK (databricks.sdk) used directly from both the Airflow DAG and the reporting/OLTP-loader modules — no separate JDBC driver management.

docs.title: Operational store: PostgreSQL (OLTP)
docs.text: Why: A relational, foreign-key-enforced schema (CORE/ENRL/UTIL — see Chapter 9) is the natural fit for application-facing enrollment reads/writes, and is intentionally kept separate from the analytical Delta star schema so analytical query load never contends with operational traffic. psycopg2 is used directly (src/medenroll834/oltp/oltp_loader.py) rather than an ORM, keeping the upsert SQL explicit and auditable.

docs.title: Object storage: S3-compatible blob storage (POC) / AWS S3 (enterprise target)
docs.text: Why: Databricks' free/serverless tier does not support a live connection to an external AWS S3 bucket, so AWS S3 was not a feasible landing layer for this proof of concept. A third-party S3-compatible blob provider was used instead for the POC's landing/archive/report storage (src/medenroll834/storage/blob_storage.py). For an enterprise deployment with a paid Databricks tier, AWS S3 is the recommended target — the interface is already implemented at src/medenroll834/s3/s3_utils.py with the equivalent upload_834 / list_landing_files / archive_834 functions, so swapping storage providers requires no change to Bronze/Silver/Gold, OLTP, OLAP, BI, or AI code.

docs.title: Containerization: Docker / Docker Compose
docs.text: Why: The full Airflow stack (webserver, scheduler, worker, Postgres metadata DB, Redis broker) is reproducible with one docker compose up -d (docker-compose.yaml), with the project bind-mounted at /opt/airflow/project so src/ and generator/ import directly into DAG tasks without a separate package build step.

docs.title: CI/CD: GitHub Actions
docs.text: Why: Free for public repos, with first-class native GitHub integration (no separate CI account/billing to provision) and a large marketplace of pre-built actions for exactly the steps this project needs (Python setup, Docker buildx/push, Codecov upload). The existing .github/workflows/ci.yml / cd.yml cover lint, test, security scan, build, and Docker image publish — see Chapter 31 for the full pipeline and a known path-configuration bug that currently needs fixing in ci.yml.

docs.text: Concern Technology Why (grounded in this repo) Distributed processing PySpark 4.0+, Delta Lake 4.0+ Scales with volume; ACID + schema evolution on Bronze/Silver/Gold Orchestration Apache Airflow 3.x (TaskFlow, Celery) Retries, task graph, Variable overrides, UI, portable open-source skill set Compute platform Databricks (Serverless-compatible) Managed Spark + Unity Catalog + SQL warehouses + databricks-sdk Operational store PostgreSQL FK-enforced OLTP schema, kept apart from OLAP OLTP driver psycopg2 (raw SQL) Explicit, auditable upsert statements Object storage (POC) S3-compatible blob storage Works on Databricks' free tier, where native AWS S3 access isn't available Object storage (enterprise) AWS S3 Same interface (s3_utils.py), swap-in only, once on a paid Databricks tier Containerization Docker / Docker Compose One-command reproducible Airflow stack CI/CD GitHub Actions Free, native GitHub integration, large action marketplace IaC Terraform S3 bucket + policy as code (04_infrastructure/01_terraform)

docs.title: 07. AWS / S3 Setup
docs.text: This chapter covers the enterprise-target AWS S3 setup (the current POC runs on S3-compatible blob storage instead — see Chapter 4, section 6). The Terraform and IAM policy below are real, committed infrastructure code already in the repo (04_infrastructure/01_terraform/), even though the runtime pipeline currently points at blob storage.

docs.title: Terraform-managed S3 bucket
docs.text:
Source: 04_infrastructure/01_terraform/main.tf

resource "aws_s3_bucket" "med834" {
  bucket = var.bucket_name
  tags = {
    Project            = "MED834ENRL"
    Environment        = "dev"
    DataClassification = "synthetic"
    ManagedBy          = "Terraform"
  }

resource "aws_s3_bucket_versioning" "med834" {

docs.text:
Source: 04_infrastructure/02_sql/03_olap/04_gold/

FACT_ENROLLMENT sits at the center, surrounded by five dimensions — all Delta tables in the GOLD schema:

CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS GOLD.FACT_ENROLLMENT (
  ENROLLMENT_FACT_KEY BIGINT GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  MEME_KEY BIGINT NOT NULL,
  PLPL_KEY BIGINT NOT NULL,

docs.text: No production member data is used anywhere in this project. All 834 files are generated by generator/synthetic_834_generator.py, which produces structurally valid X12 834 (5010) EDI files from randomized but realistic name/address/plan pools.

docs.title: Reference data pools
docs.text:
The generator draws from hard-coded, realistic-looking pools so the output resembles production data in shape without being production data:

FIRST_NAMES = ["JOHN", "JANE", "ROBERT", "MARY", ...]       # 38 names
LAST_NAMES  = ["SMITH", "JOHNSON", "WILLIAMS", ...]          # 38 names
STREET_NAMES = ["MAIN ST", "OAK AVE", "PINE RD", ...]
CITIES = ["NEW YORK", "LOS ANGELES", "CHICAGO", ...]         # 20 cities
STATES = ["AL", "AK", "AZ", ..., "WY"]                       # all 50
PLAN_CODES = ["100", "101", "102", "103", "104", "105", "106", "107"]  # plain numeric plan codes
RELATIONSHIP = ["18", "01", "03", "19"]  # self, spouse, child, domestic_partner
ADR_TYP = ["HOME", "MAILING", "BILLING", "WORK"]
GROUP_NUMBERS = [str(3300 + i) for i in range(50)]  # pure-numeric employer group pool

PLAN_TIER_NAME maps each numeric PLAN_CODE to a display tier ("100" -> "GOLD", "101" -> "SILVER", ...) for PLAN_NAME synthesis in Silver/Gold/OLAP, since the plan code itself is now opaque. PLAN_CODES is the exact set DataFrameValidator.VALID_PLANS validates against in Silver — generated files are guaranteed valid by construction unless --messy is passed (see below).

docs.title: X12 envelope construction
docs.text:
Each file is a properly-terminated X12 interchange: ISA → GS → ST → (member segments) → SE → GE → IEA, with a computed ISA checksum:

def _checksum_isa(isa_segment: str) -> str:
    total = sum(ord(c) for c in isa_segment)
    return f"{total % 256:02d}"

def build_isa(ctrl: str, file_date: str) -> str:
    body = (
        f"*00*          *00*          "
        f"*ZZ*SENDERID     *ZZ*RECEIVERID   "
        f"*{file_date}*1200*^*00501*{ctrl}*0*T*:"
    )
    checksum = _checksum_isa(body)
    return f"ISA{body}{checksum}"

Segments are ~-terminated, with a trailing newline for readability — the ~ is the real X12 record delimiter; newlines are cosmetic (and the Bronze parser's split_segments() normalizes both, see Chapter 13):

return "\n".join(s + "~" for s in [isa, gs] + segments + [se, ge, iea]) + "\n"

docs.title: Member, subscriber, and group identifiers
docs.text:
All business identifiers are now plain-digit numeric strings instead of prefixed codes (e.g. "2043434" for a member, "3341" for an employer group), matching the dbdiagram physical models under docs-site/docs/assets/architecture/physical-oltp and physical-olap:

def _numeric_id(used: set, low: int = 1000000, high: int = 9999999) -> str:
    """Unique 7-digit member/subscriber identifier, e.g. "2043434"."""
    while True:
        candidate = random.randint(low, high)
        if candidate not in used:
            used.add(candidate)
            return str(candidate)

Each subscriber is assigned a GRGR_NUM drawn from the fixed GROUP_NUMBERS pool ("3300"–"3349") and carried through the file via the X12-standard REF*1L*<group number> (Group or Policy Number) segment — the same segment Silver's _extract_ref_group_data() reads back out, so group_id is populated from real file content end-to-end instead of a hardcoded default:

def build_ref_group(grgr_num: str) -> str:
    return f"REF*1L*{grgr_num}"

docs.title: 12. 834 Parser
docs.text:
Source: src/medenroll834/parsers/edi834_parser.py

EDI834Parser is the PySpark-native entry point that turns raw 834 file content into a Bronze-shaped DataFrame. It is a thin wrapper around the same segment-splitting logic used by BronzeLayer (see Chapter 13) — the parser exists as a standalone, directly-testable class so tests can parse files without going through the full BronzeLayer.ingest() Delta-write path.

docs.title: Segment splitting
docs.text:
def split_segments(content: str) -> list:
    """Split an X12 834 payload into individual segments.

    Handles both segment conventions found in real 834 files:
    * terminator-delimited ("ISA*...~GS*...~") where "~" is the only
      record delimiter and physical newlines are cosmetic;
    * line-delimited ("ISA*...\\nGS*...\\n") which some upstream systems
      emit, where the newline is the de-facto terminator and "~" may be
      absent.

    The two are frequently mixed within a single file, so neither
    delimiter can be assumed on its own. Normalise every newline to "~"
    then split on "~" to get exactly one record per segment whatever the
    producer used.
    """
    normalised = content.replace("\r\n", "~").replace("\r", "~").replace("\n", "~")
    return [seg.strip() for seg in normalised.split("~") if seg.strip()]

This is a deliberate real-world robustness decision: production 834 feeds are not guaranteed to be consistently delimited, and this normalization means the parser never silently drops or merges segments because of a delimiter mismatch.

docs.title: Parsing a directory of files
docs.text:
def parse_files(self, landing_path: str) -> DataFrame:
    path = Path(landing_path)
    files = sorted(path.glob("*.834"))
    rows = []
    for file in files:
        content = file.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
        file_name = file.name
        for seg_order, line in enumerate(split_segments(content)):
            elements = line.split("*")
            rows.append({
                "file_name": file_name,
                "segment_id": elements[0],
                "elements": elements,
                "raw_segment": line,
                "seg_order": seg_order,
            })
    return self.spark.createDataFrame(rows, schema=BRONZE_SCHEMA)

Each X12 segment is split on * into its data elements; elements[0] is always the segment identifier (ISA, GS, ST, HL, NM1, INS, DTP, HD, N3, N4, REF, SE, GE, IEA). seg_order preserves the segment's original position within the file — critical because downstream Silver logic resolves hierarchy and "most recent value" using window functions ordered by this column.

docs.title: Schema
docs.text:
BRONZE_SCHEMA = StructType([
    StructField("file_name", StringType(), True),
    StructField("segment_id", StringType(), True),
    StructField("elements", ArrayType(StringType()), True),
    StructField("raw_segment", StringType(), True),
    StructField("seg_order", LongType(), True),
])

elements is kept as an array of strings, not individually typed columns — this is what lets a single Bronze schema represent every segment type without a different column set per segment, at the cost of pushing positional extraction (elements[8] for a member ID, etc.) into Silver.

RELATIONSHIP_MAP = {
    "18": "self",
    "01": "spouse",
    "03": "child",
    "19": "domestic_partner",
}

docs.title: 13. Bronze Layer
docs.text:
Source: src/medenroll834/ingestion/bronze.py

The Bronze layer is the raw, untransformed landing zone: one row per X12 segment, schema fixed, content untouched beyond splitting into elements. Its job is to preserve the source data exactly as received, so every downstream transformation can be replayed or audited against it.

docs.title: BronzeLayer.ingest()
docs.text:
class BronzeLayer:
    def __init__(self, spark: SparkSession, config: Dict):
        self.spark = spark
        self.config = config

    def ingest(self, landing_path: str) -> DataFrame:
        self.logger = setup_logging("bronze")
        start_time = log_pipeline_start(self.logger, "BRONZE", f"landing_path={landing_path}")

        path = Path(landing_path)
        files = sorted(path.glob("*.834"))
        rows = []
        try:
            for file in files:
                content = file.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
                file_name = file.name
                for seg_order, line in enumerate(split_segments(content)):
                    elements = line.split("*")
                    rows.append({
                        "file_name": file_name,
                        "segment_id": elements[0],
                        "elements": elements,
                        "raw_segment": line,
                        "seg_order": seg_order,
                    })

            parsed = self.spark.createDataFrame(rows, schema=BRONZE_SCHEMA)
            parsed = parsed.withColumn("ingested_at", F.current_timestamp().cast("string"))

            table_path = self.config["layers"]["bronze"]["path"]
            (
                parsed.write.format("delta")
                .mode("overwrite")
                .option("mergeSchema", "true")
                .option("delta.autoOptimize.optimizeWrite", "true")
                .save(table_path)
            )
        except Exception:
            log_pipeline_error(self.logger, "BRONZE", f"landing_path={landing_path}", start_time)
            raise

        result_count = parsed.count()
        log_pipeline_end(self.logger, "BRONZE", f"segments_loaded={result_count}", start_time)
        return parsed

docs.title: Write semantics
docs.text: Option Value Why mode overwrite Each pipeline run ingests the current landing directory's files as a fresh Bronze snapshot mergeSchema true Tolerates schema drift (e.g. an added column) without a manual ALTER TABLE delta.autoOptimize.optimizeWrite true Compacts small files at write time — important because 834 ingestion produces many small per-file row batches

docs.title: Output schema
docs.text:
BRONZE_SCHEMA = StructType([
    StructField("file_name", StringType(), True),
    StructField("segment_id", StringType(), True),
    StructField("elements", ArrayType(StringType()), True),
    StructField("raw_segment", StringType(), True),
    StructField("seg_order", LongType(), True),
    StructField("ingested_at", StringType(), True),
])

Stored at the Delta path configured in 03_config/pipeline_config.yaml:

layers:
  bronze:
    path: 10_data/bronze/edi834_segments
    table: bronze_edi_segments
    format: delta
    options:
      mergeSchema: "true"
      delta.autoOptimize.optimizeWrite: "true"

On Databricks, the equivalent table is med834enrl.edi.bronze_edi_segments (see 04_infrastructure/02_sql/01_delta/bronze_edi_segments.sql).

docs.title: Databricks notebook equivalent
docs.text:
The production Databricks job (05_orchestration/databricks/med834_medallion_job.py) implements the same Bronze logic using read_files() SQL + explode() instead of a Python loop over local files, because it reads from a Unity Catalog Volume rather than the local filesystem:

raw = spark.sql(
    f"SELECT value, element_at(split(_metadata.file_path, '/'), -1) AS file_name "
    f"FROM read_files('{LANDING}', format => 'text', wholeText => true)"
)
bronze = (
    raw.withColumn("segment", F.explode(F.split(F.regexp_replace("value", r"[\r\n]+", "~"), "~")))
    .filter(F.trim("segment") != "")
    .withColumn("elements", F.split(F.col("segment"), r"\*"))
    .withColumn("segment_id", F.element_at("elements", 1))
    .withColumn("seg_order", F.monotonically_increasing_id())
    .withColumn("raw_segment", F.col("segment"))
    .withColumn("ingested_at", F.current_timestamp())
    .select("file_name", "segment_id", "elements", "raw_segment", "seg_order", "ingested_at")
)
bronze.write.format("delta").mode("overwrite").option("overwriteSchema", "true") \
    .saveAsTable(f"{EDI}.bronze_edi_segments")

Same segment-normalization idea (~/newline → ~), same per-segment elements array shape — just expressed in distributed SQL/DataFrame operations instead of a Python-side file loop, because read_files() and explode() are what scale across a Databricks cluster reading many files from a Volume at once.

docs.title: Pipeline summary contribution
docs.text:
BronzeLayer.ingest()'s row count feeds directly into the DeltaMedallionPipeline.run() summary dict (see Chapter 18):

summary = {
    "bronze_segments": bronze_df.count(),
    ...
}

docs.title: 14. Silver Layer
docs.text:
Source: src/medenroll834/ingestion/silver.py

The Silver layer turns raw Bronze segments into one normalized row per member, resolving the X12 HL (hierarchical level) structure, extracting every relevant segment type, formatting dates, and applying validation — all as Spark DataFrame/window operations, with no row-by-row Python loops on the member data itself.

docs.title: Why HL resolution is hard (and how it's solved)
docs.text:
X12 834 files model subscriber/dependent relationships through HL segments: HL*<id>*<parent_id>*<level>*<child_count>. The catch, documented directly in the code, is that HL ids are only unique within a transaction set (each ST*834.../SE pair restarts numbering at 1) — not within the whole file:

# HL ids are only unique *within a transaction set* (each ST*834.../SE
# pair restarts numbering at 1), not within the file. A file with 100
# enrolments contains 100 HL rows with hl_id=1, so resolving dependents
# against subscribers on hl_id alone matches every subscriber in the
# file and fans out 100x.

The fix is a transaction-scoped key, derived by carrying the most recent ST row forward with a window function:

file_order = Window.partitionBy("file_name").orderBy(F.col("seg_row"))
ordered = ordered.withColumn(
    "txn_row",
    F.last(
        F.when(F.col("segment_id") == "ST", F.col("seg_row")),
        ignorenulls=True,
    ).over(file_order.rowsBetween(Window.unboundedPreceding, Window.currentRow)),
)
ordered = ordered.withColumn(
    "hl_key",
    F.concat_ws("-", F.col("file_name"), F.col("txn_row").cast("string")),
)

An earlier version range-joined against every ST row instead, which matched a segment to all preceding transaction sets and multiplied member rows ~5x. last() over a cumulative window yields exactly one key per segment.

docs.title: Deriving member row ranges from HL boundaries
docs.text:
Each HL segment marks the start of one member's data block; the next HL segment (within the same transaction) marks the end:

hl_window = Window.partitionBy("hl_key").orderBy(F.col("seg_row"))
hl_with_next = hl_events.withColumn(
    "next_hl_row", F.lead("seg_row").over(hl_window)
).fillna(999999999, subset=["next_hl_row"])
## Segment extraction (NM1, INS, DTP, HD, EB, N3/N4, REF)

Each segment type is extracted with its own `groupBy(...).agg(F.max(F.when(...)))`
helper, keyed on `(file_name, seg_start)` — the member block identifier:

```python
def _extract_nm1_data(self, members_df):
    nm1_seg = members_df.filter(F.col("segment_id") == "NM1")
    return nm1_seg.groupBy("file_name", "seg_start", "hl_level").agg(
        F.max(F.when(F.col("elements")[1] == "IL", F.col("elements")[2])).alias("last_name"),
        F.max(F.when(F.col("elements")[1] == "IL", F.col("elements")[3])).alias("first_name"),
        F.max(F.when(F.col("elements")[1] == "IL", F.col("elements")[8])).alias("member_id"),
    )
Helper Segment Extracts _extract_nm1_data NM1 last name, first name, member id (entity code IL) _extract_ins_data INS relationship (via RELATIONSHIP_MAP; subscriber is hardcoded "self") _extract_dtp_data DTP DOB (291), coverage start (472/348), coverage end (349) _extract_hd_data HD plan id _extract_eb_data EB fallback coverage start/end (coalesced if DTP is absent) _extract_address_data N3/N4/REF*2L street/city/state/zip, resolved to the member via the nearest preceding REF*2L

docs.title: Subscriber resolution without a fan-out join
docs.text:
HL level 20 = subscriber, level 21 = dependent. A dependent must be tied to its subscriber's member_id. The naive approach — a self-join on hl_parent_id == hl_id — duplicated every dependent against every candidate subscriber and blew the executor heap. The fix is a broadcast map built from a small collect():

# Implemented with a broadcast map rather than a self-join. A join here
# duplicated every dependent against every candidate subscriber and
# blew the executor heap; a broadcast lookup is O(1) per row and cannot
# fan out because the key set is collapsed with first().
subscriber_map = {
    f"{r['hl_key']}|{r['hl_id']}": r["member_id"]
    for r in base.filter(F.col("is_subscriber"))
    .select("hl_key", "hl_id", "member_id")
    .dropDuplicates(["hl_key", "hl_id"])
    .collect()
}
subscriber_lookup = F.create_map(*[item for kv in subscriber_map.items() for item in (F.lit(kv[0]), F.lit(kv[1]))])
base = base.withColumn(
    "subscriber_id",
    F.when(F.col("is_subscriber"), F.col("member_id"))
     .otherwise(F.element_at(subscriber_lookup, F.concat_ws("|", F.col("hl_key"), F.col("hl_parent_id")))),
)

This only collect()s the (small) set of distinct subscribers, not the full member population, so it scales with group count rather than member

docs.title: Date formatting
docs.text:
X12 dates arrive as YYYYMMDD strings; Silver reformats them to YYYY-MM-DD:

def _format_date(self, col_name: str):
    return F.when(
        (F.length(F.col(col_name)) == 8) & F.col(col_name).rlike(r"^\d{8}$"),
        F.concat(F.substring(F.col(col_name), 1, 4), F.lit("-"),
                  F.substring(F.col(col_name), 5, 2), F.lit("-"),
                  F.substring(F.col(col_name), 7, 2)),
    ).otherwise(F.col(col_name))

docs.text:
SILVER_SCHEMA adds hl_id, hl_parent_id, subscriber_id, address_member_id, validation_errors, and is_valid on top of the flattened member attributes — see 04_infrastructure/02_sql/01_delta/silver_members.sql for the Delta table DDL. Written with delta.deletedFileRetentionDuration: "interval 7 days" per pipeline_config.yaml, giving a 7-day time-travel window for debugging.

See Chapter 15 for how Gold consumes is_subscriber/subscriber_id, and Chapter 16 for _apply_validation().

```

A range join (seg_row >= seg_start AND seg_row < seg_end) then attaches every segment between consecutive HLs to the right member block.

docs.title: 15. Business Rules / Plan Assignment
docs.text: This chapter covers how a member is assigned to a benefit plan and rolled up under the correct subscriber/group — the pipeline's core "enrollment business rule" logic, spread across Silver (HD segment extraction, HL resolution) and Gold (subscriber_id finalization).

docs.title: Where the plan code comes from
docs.text:
The HD (Health Coverage) segment carries the plan identifier. Silver's _extract_hd_data() (see Chapter 14) pulls element index 3 directly as the plan code:

def _extract_hd_data(self, members_df):
    hd_seg = members_df.filter(F.col("segment_id") == "HD")
    return hd_seg.groupBy("file_name", "seg_start").agg(
        F.max(F.col("elements")[3]).alias("plan_code"),
    ).withColumn("plan_id", F.col("plan_code")).select("file_name", "seg_start", "plan_id")

docs.title: Valid plan codes (the business rule)
docs.text:
The complete set of accepted plan products is defined once and shared between the generator, the validator, and pipeline_config.yaml:

VALID_PLANS = {"100", "101", "102", "103", "104", "105", "106", "107"}

# 03_config/pipeline_config.yaml
validation:
  require_plan_code: true
  valid_plan_codes:
    - "100"
    - "101"
    - "102"
    - "103"
    - "104"
    - "105"
    - "106"
    - "107"

Any plan_id outside this set produces a validation error ("Unknown plan: <code>") and the row is quarantined — see Chapter 16.

docs.title: Relationship-driven subscriber assignment
docs.text:
Plan assignment is not just "attach a plan code" — it must correctly determine whose enrollment record a plan applies to, by resolving the X12 relationship hierarchy:

RELATIONSHIP_MAP = {
    "18": "self",              # subscriber (primary policyholder)
    "01": "spouse",             # dependent
    "03": "child",               # dependent
    "19": "domestic_partner",   # dependent
}

HL level 20 always means subscriber; level 21 always means dependent. Silver materializes is_subscriber directly from this, because Gold's plan/group roll-up depends on it:

# HL level 20 = subscriber, 21 = dependent. Gold depends on this flag to
# roll dependents up to their subscriber, so it must be materialised
# here; leaving it null silently produces null group_id in Gold.
base = base.withColumn(
    "is_subscriber",
    F.when(F.col("hl_level") == "20", F.lit(True)).otherwise(F.lit(False)),
)

docs.title: Gold finalizes the subscriber assignment
docs.text:
Source: src/medenroll834/ingestion/gold.py

gold_df = (
    silver_df.withColumn(
        "subscriber_id",
        F.when(F.col("is_subscriber"), F.col("member_id")).otherwise(
            F.col("subscriber_id")
        ),
    )
    .filter(F.col("is_valid") == True)
    .dropDuplicates(["file_name", "member_id"])
    ...
)

This is a correction over an earlier version that joined on group_id — which Silver had actually populated from the REF*2L address-association key (a member id, not a group id). That join both failed to resolve correctly and fanned out rows. Because subscriber_id is already resolved in Silver via the HL hierarchy (see Chapter 14), Gold does no re-derivation and no positional guesswork — it only finalizes the subscriber's own row to point at itself.

docs.title: Enrollment maintenance type (OLTP load)
docs.text:
When loading into the OLTP CORE schema, every enrollment event is written with a fixed maintenance type code "021" (addition) and an enrl_stat of "ACTIVE":

cur.execute(
    "INSERT INTO core.core_meen_enrollment (meme_id, plpl_id, txn_id, maint_typ_cd, "
    "eff_dt, term_dt, enrl_stat, crtd_ts, updt_ts) VALUES (%s,%s,%s,%s,%s,%s,%s,%s,%s)",
    (meme_id, plpl_id, txn_id, "021", _as_date(r.get("coverage_start_date")) or now.date(),
     _as_date_open_ended(r.get("coverage_end_date")),
     "ACTIVE" if _as_date(r.get("coverage_end_date")) is None else "TERMED", now, now),
)

_as_date_open_ended() replaces a missing/NULL coverage end date with the fixed 9999-12-31 sentinel (OPEN_ENDED_DATE) instead of NULL, so term_dt/END_DATE is always a real, queryable date across both OLTP and OLAP (see Chapter 19).

The OLAP FACT_ENROLLMENT builder in the Databricks notebook derives ENROLLMENT_STATUS dynamically instead, based on whether a coverage end date is present:

.withColumn("ENROLLMENT_STATUS",
    F.when(F.col("coverage_end_date").isNull() | (F.col("coverage_end_date") == ""),
           F.lit("ACTIVE")).otherwise(F.lit("TERMED")))

See Chapter 17 and Chapter 19 for the full downstream loads.

docs.title: 16. Data Quality & Reject Handling
docs.text: MedEnroll834 validates every member record with Spark-SQL expressions (no row-by-row Python), tags each row with its specific failure reasons, and routes invalid rows to a dedicated Delta quarantine table instead of dropping or silently failing them.

docs.title: Validation rules
docs.text:
Source: src/medenroll834/quality/validator.py (standalone) and SilverLayer._apply_validation() (inline, identical logic)

class DataFrameValidator:
    VALID_PLANS = {"100", "101", "102", "103", "104", "105", "106", "107"}

    def validate(self, df: DataFrame) -> DataFrame:
        errors = F.filter(
            F.array(
                F.when(F.col("member_id") == "", F.lit("Member ID is required")),
                F.when(F.col("first_name") == "", F.lit("First name is required")),
                F.when(F.col("last_name") == "", F.lit("Last name is required")),
                F.when(F.col("plan_id") == "", F.lit("Plan ID is required")),
                F.when(
                    (F.col("coverage_start_date").isNotNull()) & (F.col("coverage_end_date").isNotNull()),
                    F.when(F.try_to_date(F.col("coverage_start_date")) > F.try_to_date(F.col("coverage_end_date")),
                           F.lit("Coverage start after end")),
                ),
                F.when(
                    (F.col("date_of_birth").isNotNull()) & (F.col("coverage_start_date").isNotNull()),
                    F.when(F.try_to_date(F.col("coverage_start_date")) < F.try_to_date(F.col("date_of_birth")),
                           F.lit("Coverage before DOB")),
                ),
                F.when(~F.col("plan_id").isin(list(self.VALID_PLANS)),
                       F.concat(F.lit("Unknown plan: "), F.col("plan_id"))),
            ),
            lambda x: x.isNotNull(),
        )
        return df.withColumn("validation_errors", errors).withColumn(
            "is_valid", F.size(F.col("validation_errors")) == 0
        )

docs.title: The six validation rules
docs.text:
# Rule Error message 1 member_id required Member ID is required 2 first_name required First name is required 3 last_name required Last name is required 4 plan_id required Plan ID is required 5 coverage start ≤ coverage end (when both present) Coverage start after end 6 coverage start ≥ date of birth (when both present) Coverage before DOB 7 plan_id is one of the 8 valid plan codes Unknown plan: <code>

Each row can accumulate multiple errors at once — validation_errors is an array, not a single flag, so a reject-remediation team sees every problem with a record in one place rather than fixing issues one at a time across repeated pipeline runs. F.try_to_date() is used (not F.to_date()) so a malformed date string produces null and is excluded from the comparison rather than crashing the whole DataFrame evaluation.

docs.title: is_valid flag
docs.text:
.withColumn("is_valid", F.size(F.col("validation_errors")) == 0)

A row is valid if and only if its error array is empty — this single boolean is what the pipeline orchestrator (DeltaMedallionPipeline.run()) and the Gold layer filter on.

docs.title: Quarantine routing
docs.text:
Source: src/medenroll834/quality/quarantine.py

class DeltaQuarantineManager:
    def write_invalid(self, invalid_df: DataFrame) -> None:
        quarantine_df = invalid_df.withColumn(
            "quarantined_at", F.current_timestamp().cast("string")
        ).withColumn("quarantine_id", F.expr("uuid()"))

        table_path = self.config["quarantine"]["path"]
        (
            quarantine_df.write.format("delta")
            .mode("append")
            .option("mergeSchema", "true")
            .save(table_path)
        )

Quarantine writes are appended, not overwritten — every run's rejects accumulate historically, each tagged with a unique quarantine_id and a quarantined_at timestamp, so a remediation team can audit when and how often a given record kept failing.

docs.title: Where quarantine fits in the pipeline
docs.text:
# src/medenroll834/ingestion/pipeline.py
bronze_df = self.bronze.ingest(landing_path)
silver_df = self.silver.transform(bronze_df)
gold_df = self.gold.transform(silver_df)

valid_df = silver_df.filter(F.col("is_valid") == True)
invalid_df = silver_df.filter(F.col("is_valid") == False)
self.quarantine.write_invalid(invalid_df)

Quarantine operates on the Silver output (after HL resolution and field extraction, before Gold deduplication/enrichment) — so a quarantined record retains all the context Silver resolved about it (relationship, subscriber hierarchy, address) even though it failed validation, which makes remediation easier than quarantining raw Bronze segments.

docs.title: OLTP-side rejects (ENRL_RJRW_REJECT)
docs.text:
The OLTP schema has a parallel reject concept at the operational layer:

CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS ENRL.ENRL_RJRW_REJECT (
  RJRW_ID BIGINT GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  TXN_ID BIGINT NOT NULL,
  SRC_ROW TEXT NOT NULL,
  RJCT_CD VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
  RJCT_RSN VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
  RJCT_TS TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL
);

FK'd to ENRL_EDXN_TRANSACTION, so every reject traces back to the specific inbound file transaction it came from — the OLTP equivalent of the Delta quarantine table's file_name/quarantine_id lineage.

docs.title: Pipeline run summary
docs.text:
Quarantine counts are surfaced directly in the pipeline's return value, so reject volume is visible without a separate query:

    "bronze_segments": bronze_df.count(),
    "silver_total": silver_df.count(),
    "silver_valid": valid_df.count(),
    "silver_invalid": invalid_df.count(),
    "gold_records": gold_df.count(),

docs.title: 17. PostgreSQL Bulk Load / Upsert
docs.text:
Source: src/medenroll834/oltp/oltp_loader.py

load_gold_to_oltp() reads the Databricks Gold table via a SQL warehouse and writes it into the PostgreSQL CORE/ENRL schemas, using natural-key upserts so re-running the load does not duplicate reference data (groups, plans, subscribers).

docs.title: Reading Gold from Databricks
docs.text:
GOLD_TABLE = "med834enrl.edi.gold_enrollments"

def _read_gold_from_databricks(warehouse_id=None, profile=None) -> List[Dict]:
    from databricks.sdk import WorkspaceClient
    from databricks.sdk.service.sql import StatementState

    w = WorkspaceClient(**({"profile": profile} if profile else {}))
    if not warehouse_id:
        whs = list(w.warehouses.list())
        warehouse_id = whs[0].id

    sql = (
        "SELECT member_id, first_name, last_name, date_of_birth, gender, "
        "group_id, group_name, plan_id, coverage_start_date, coverage_end_date, "
        "street_1, street_2, city, state, zip_code, relationship, is_subscriber, "
        f"file_name FROM {GOLD_TABLE}"
    )
    resp = w.statement_execution.execute_statement(
        warehouse_id=warehouse_id, statement=sql, wait_timeout="50s"
    )
    while resp.status.state in (StatementState.PENDING, StatementState.RUNNING):
        time.sleep(2)
        resp = w.statement_execution.get_statement(resp.statement_id)
    if resp.status.state != StatementState.SUCCEEDED:
        raise RuntimeError(f"Gold read failed: {resp.status.error.message}")

    cols = [c.name for c in resp.manifest.schema.columns]
    return [dict(zip(cols, r)) for r in (resp.result.data_array or [])]

Uses the databricks-sdk's SQL Statement Execution API — no JDBC driver, no cluster to keep warm; the serverless SQL warehouse spins up on demand.

docs.title: The load: one transaction, natural-key upserts
docs.text:
def load_gold_to_oltp(oltp_db_url=None, warehouse_id=None, databricks_profile=None, rows=None) -> Dict:
    oltp_db_url = oltp_db_url or os.environ["OLTP_DATABASE_URL"]
    if rows is None:
        rows = _read_gold_from_databricks(warehouse_id, databricks_profile)

    conn = psycopg2.connect(oltp_db_url)
    conn.autocommit = False
    cur = conn.cursor()
    loaded = {"groups": 0, "plans": 0, "subscribers": 0, "members": 0,
              "addresses": 0, "transactions": 0, "enrollments": 0}
    try:
        # ... per-row processing (below) ...
        conn.commit()
    except Exception:
        conn.rollback()
        raise
    finally:
        cur.close()
        conn.close()
    return loaded

The entire load runs in one transaction — any failure partway through rolls back everything, so the OLTP database never ends up with a half-loaded file's data.

docs.title: Upsert pattern (ON CONFLICT ... DO UPDATE)
docs.text:
Reference entities (group, plan, subscriber) are upserted on their natural key, with an in-memory cache (group_cache, plan_cache) to avoid redundant round-trips within the same load:

if grp_num not in group_cache:
    cur.execute(
        "INSERT INTO core.core_grgr_group (grgr_num, st_cd, eff_dt, crtd_ts, updt_ts) "
        "VALUES (%s,%s,%s,%s,%s) ON CONFLICT (grgr_num) DO UPDATE SET updt_ts=EXCLUDED.updt_ts "
        "RETURNING grgr_id",
        (grp_num, (r.get("state") or "NA")[:2], _as_date(r.get("coverage_start_date")) or now.date(), now, now),
    )
    group_cache[grp_num] = cur.fetchone()[0]

This is why the loader is idempotent: re-running it against the same Gold data updates updt_ts on existing groups/plans/subscribers instead of inserting duplicates — see Chapter 22.

docs.title: Member and enrollment inserts (not upserted)
docs.text:
core_meme_member and core_meen_enrollment are plain inserts — a member row is created fresh for each processed Gold record (member identity is owned by the subscriber's natural key + relationship code, not a separately upserted key in this simplified schema):

cur.execute(
    "INSERT INTO core.core_meme_member (mesb_id, rltn_cd, fst_nm, lst_nm, dob, gndr_cd, "
    "is_act, crtd_ts, updt_ts) VALUES (%s,%s,%s,%s,%s,%s,%s,%s,%s) RETURNING meme_id",
    (mesb_id, _rel_code(r.get("relationship")), ..., True, now, now),
)
meme_id = cur.fetchone()[0]

docs.title: One transaction row created per file
docs.text:
for file_nm in {r["file_name"] for r in rows if r.get("file_name")}:
    cur.execute(
        "INSERT INTO enrl.enrl_edxn_transaction "
        "(file_nm, isa_ctrl_num, gs_ctrl_num, st_ctrl_num, sndr_id, rcvr_id, "
        "rcvd_ts, proc_stat, rec_cnt) VALUES (%s,%s,%s,%s,%s,%s,%s,%s,%s) RETURNING txn_id",
        (file_nm, "N/A", "N/A", "N/A", "SENDERID", "RECEIVERID", now, "PROCESSED", 0),
    )

file_txn maps each file name to its transaction id, so every core_meen_enrollment row can be FK'd back to the specific 834 file it came from — this is the OLTP-side equivalent of Gold's file_name lineage column.

docs.title: Helper conversions
docs.text:
def _as_date(value):
    """Try YYYY-MM-DD then YYYYMMDD; returns None if neither parses."""
    ...

def _rel_code(relationship):
    """Reverse-maps Silver's relationship string back to the X12 code (e.g. 'spouse' -> '01')."""
    mapping = {"self": "18", "spouse": "01", "child": "03", "domestic_partner": "19"}
    return mapping.get((relationship or "self").lower(), "18")

docs.title: 18. Gold Layer
docs.text:
Source: src/medenroll834/ingestion/gold.py

The Gold layer is the final, analytics-ready output: deduplicated, valid-only enrollment records with derived convenience fields, written with Change Data Feed enabled so downstream consumers (OLAP star schema builder, OLTP loader) can read incrementally in the future.

docs.title: Full transform
docs.text:
class GoldLayer:
    def transform(self, silver_df: DataFrame) -> DataFrame:
        self.logger = setup_logging("gold")
        start_time = log_pipeline_start(self.logger, "GOLD", "transforming silver to gold")

        try:
            gold_df = (
                silver_df.withColumn(
                    "subscriber_id",
                    F.when(F.col("is_subscriber"), F.col("member_id")).otherwise(
                        F.col("subscriber_id")
                    ),
                )
                .filter(F.col("is_valid") == True)
                .dropDuplicates(["file_name", "member_id"])
                .withColumn("full_name", F.concat_ws(" ", F.col("first_name"), F.col("last_name")))
                .withColumn(
                    "age_years",
                    F.floor(F.datediff(F.current_date(), F.to_date(F.col("date_of_birth"), "yyyy-MM-dd")) / 365.25),
                )
                .withColumn("ingested_at", F.current_timestamp().cast("string"))
            )

            table_path = self.config["layers"]["gold"]["path"]
            (
                gold_df.write.format("delta")
                .mode("overwrite")
                .option("mergeSchema", "true")
                .option("delta.enableChangeDataFeed", "true")
                .save(table_path)
            )
        except Exception:
            log_pipeline_error(self.logger, "GOLD", "transforming silver to gold", start_time)
            raise

        log_pipeline_end(self.logger, "GOLD", f"records={gold_df.count()}", start_time)
        return gold_df

docs.title: What Gold does, step by step
docs.text:
1. Finalize subscriber_id — see Chapter 15 for why this does no re-derivation from group_id (a past bug).
  2. Filter to is_valid == True — invalid rows never reach Gold; they were already routed to quarantine from Silver (see Chapter 16).
  3. Deduplicate on (file_name, member_id) — guards against the same member appearing twice within one file (e.g. duplicate HL blocks from a malformed or re-sent 834).
  4. Derive full_name — concat_ws(" ", first_name, last_name), a display convenience not present in Silver.
  5. Derive age_years — floor(datediff(today, dob) / 365.25), accounting for leap years via the 365.25 divisor rather than a flat 365.
  6. Write with Change Data Feed enabled — delta.enableChangeDataFeed lets a future incremental consumer read only the rows that changed since a given version, instead of re-scanning the whole Gold table.

docs.title: Write semantics
docs.text:
Option Value Why mode overwrite Gold reflects the current full state of valid enrollments per run mergeSchema true Tolerates schema drift from upstream Silver changes delta.enableChangeDataFeed true Enables future incremental/CDC-style consumption

Configured path (03_config/pipeline_config.yaml):

layers:
  gold:
    path: 10_data/gold/enrollments
    table: gold_enrollments
    format: delta
    options:
      mergeSchema: "true"
      delta.enableChangeDataFeed: "true"

On Databricks, this is med834enrl.edi.gold_enrollments — the table read by both the OLTP loader (_read_gold_from_databricks) and the report generator's REPORT_QUERIES (see Chapter 27).

docs.title: 19. OLAP Star Schema
docs.text:
Source: 05_orchestration/databricks/med834_medallion_job.py (section # ---------- OLAP star-schema dimensions ----------)

The OLAP star schema is built directly in the Databricks notebook job, immediately after the medallion Bronze/Silver/Gold run, from the same gold_enrollments table. FACT_ENROLLMENT sits at the center, surrounded by five dimensions — see Chapter 9 for the full DDL and ERD.

docs.title: Dimension builds (all SCD Type 2-shaped via CURRENT_FLAG)
docs.text:
g = spark.table(f"{EDI}.gold_enrollments")

# DIM_PLAN - PLAN_TIER_NAME maps the numeric plan code (e.g. "100") to a
# readable tier label ("GOLD", "SILVER", ...) for PLAN_NAME synthesis.
(g.select(F.col("plan_id").alias("PLPL_ID"), F.col("plan_id").alias("PLAN_CODE"),
          F.concat(F.coalesce(PLAN_TIER_NAME[F.col("plan_id")], F.col("plan_id")), F.lit(" Plan")).alias("PLAN_NAME"))
  .withColumn("LINE_OF_BUSINESS_CODE", F.lit("COMMERCIAL")).dropDuplicates(["PLPL_ID"])
  .withColumn("EFFECTIVE_DATE", F.current_date()).withColumn("END_DATE", F.to_date(F.lit("9999-12-31")))
  .withColumn("CURRENT_FLAG", F.lit(True))
  .write.format("delta").mode("overwrite").option("mergeSchema", "true").saveAsTable(f"{GOLD}.dim_plan"))

# DIM_GROUP - GRGR_ID/GROUP_NUMBER come from the REF*1L group number captured
# in Silver, not a hardcoded default.
(g.select(F.col("group_id").alias("GRGR_ID"), F.col("group_id").alias("GROUP_NUMBER"),
          F.col("group_name").alias("GROUP_NAME"), F.col("state").alias("STATE_CODE")).dropDuplicates(["GRGR_ID"])
  .withColumn("EFFECTIVE_DATE", F.current_date()).withColumn("END_DATE", F.to_date(F.lit("9999-12-31")))
  .withColumn("CURRENT_FLAG", F.lit(True))
  .write.format("delta").mode("overwrite").option("mergeSchema", "true").saveAsTable(f"{GOLD}.dim_group"))

# DIM_MEMBER
(g.select(F.col("member_id").alias("MEME_ID"), F.col("member_id").alias("MESB_ID"),
          F.col("first_name").alias("FIRST_NAME"), F.col("last_name").alias("LAST_NAME"),
          F.to_date("date_of_birth", "yyyyMMdd").alias("DATE_OF_BIRTH"), F.col("gender").alias("GENDER_CODE"),
          F.lit("18").alias("RELATIONSHIP_CODE")).dropDuplicates(["MEME_ID"])
  .withColumn("EFFECTIVE_DATE", F.current_date()).withColumn("END_DATE", F.to_date(F.lit("9999-12-31")))
  .withColumn("CURRENT_FLAG", F.lit(True))
  .write.format("delta").mode("overwrite").option("mergeSchema", "true").saveAsTable(f"{GOLD}.dim_member"))

END_DATE is never NULL — an active/open-ended dimension row stores the fixed 9999-12-31 sentinel instead, so "no end date yet" is a real, queryable date rather than NULL (see Chapter 9).

docs.title: DIM_DATE — generated date spine
docs.text:
Rather than hardcoding a date range, DIM_DATE is generated to span the actual min/max coverage dates seen in Gold, padded by a year on each side:

date_bounds = g.select(
    F.to_date("coverage_start_date", "yyyyMMdd").alias("d1"),
    F.to_date("coverage_end_date", "yyyyMMdd").alias("d2"),
).agg(F.min("d1").alias("min_d"), F.max(F.greatest("d1", "d2")).alias("max_d")).first()
min_d = (date_bounds["min_d"] or today) - timedelta(days=365)
max_d = (date_bounds["max_d"] or today) + timedelta(days=365)

dim_date = (
    spark.sql(f"SELECT explode(sequence(to_date('{min_d}'), to_date('{max_d}'), interval 1 day)) AS FULL_DATE")
    .withColumn("DATE_KEY", F.date_format("FULL_DATE", "yyyyMMdd").cast("int"))
    .withColumn("YEAR_NUMBER", F.year("FULL_DATE"))
    .withColumn("QUARTER_NUMBER", F.quarter("FULL_DATE"))
    .withColumn("MONTH_NUMBER", F.month("FULL_DATE"))
    .withColumn("DAY_NUMBER", F.dayofmonth("FULL_DATE"))
    .withColumn("DAY_OF_WEEK_NAME", F.date_format("FULL_DATE", "EEEE"))
)

DATE_KEY is an INT in YYYYMMDD form (e.g. 20260827), matching the surrogate-key convention documented in the table comment: 'DATE_KEY uses YYYYMMDD format (e.g., 20260827 = 27-Aug-2026)'.

A fixed sentinel row is appended with DATE_KEY = 99991231 / FULL_DATE = 9999-12-31 / DAY_OF_WEEK_NAME = "Open Ended", so FACT_ENROLLMENT.COVERAGE_END_DATE_KEY always has a valid DIM_DATE row to join against even for open-ended coverage — see below.

docs.title: DIM_TRANSACTION_SOURCE — hashed file identity
docs.text:
dim_txn_src = (
    g.select("file_name").dropDuplicates()
    .withColumn("TXN_ID", F.abs(F.xxhash64("file_name")))
    .withColumn("FILE_NAME", F.col("file_name"))
    .withColumn("SENDER_ID", F.lit("SENDERID"))
    .withColumn("RECEIVED_TIMESTAMP", F.current_timestamp())
)
dim_txn_src.write.format("delta").mode("overwrite").option("mergeSchema", "true") \
    .saveAsTable(f"{GOLD}.dim_transaction_source")

xxhash64 deterministically derives a numeric TXN_ID from the file name, so the same file always maps to the same transaction-source key across runs without needing a separate sequence/lookup table.

docs.title: FACT_ENROLLMENT — resolving surrogate keys
docs.text:
The fact table is built by joining Gold against the current row of each dimension (CURRENT_FLAG = true) on natural keys, then selecting only the surrogate keys:

dim_member_cur = spark.table(f"{GOLD}.dim_member").filter("CURRENT_FLAG = true") \
    .select(F.col("MEME_KEY"), F.col("MEME_ID").alias("jk_meme_id"))
dim_plan_cur = spark.table(f"{GOLD}.dim_plan").filter("CURRENT_FLAG = true") \
    .select(F.col("PLPL_KEY"), F.col("PLPL_ID").alias("jk_plpl_id"))
# ... dim_group_cur, dim_txn_tbl similarly ...

fact = (
    g.withColumn("jk_cov_start_key", F.date_format(F.to_date("coverage_start_date", "yyyyMMdd"), "yyyyMMdd").cast("int"))
     # Open-ended coverage resolves to the 9999-12-31 sentinel key instead of NULL
     .withColumn("jk_cov_end_key", F.coalesce(
         F.date_format(F.to_date("coverage_end_date", "yyyyMMdd"), "yyyyMMdd").cast("int"),
         F.lit(99991231),
     ))
     .join(dim_member_cur, F.col("member_id") == F.col("jk_meme_id"), "left").drop("jk_meme_id")
     .join(dim_plan_cur, F.col("plan_id") == F.col("jk_plpl_id"), "left").drop("jk_plpl_id")
     .join(dim_group_cur, F.col("group_id") == F.col("jk_grgr_id"), "left").drop("jk_grgr_id")
     .join(dim_txn_tbl, F.col("file_name") == F.col("jk_file_name"), "left").drop("jk_file_name")
     .join(dim_date_start, F.col("jk_cov_start_key") == F.col("start_date_key"), "left")
     .join(dim_date_end, F.col("jk_cov_end_key") == F.col("end_date_key"), "left")
     .withColumn("MAINTENANCE_TYPE_CODE", F.lit("021"))
     .withColumn("ENROLLMENT_STATUS",
         F.when(F.col("coverage_end_date").isNull() | (F.col("coverage_end_date") == ""),
                F.lit("ACTIVE")).otherwise(F.lit("TERMED")))
     .withColumn("ENROLLMENT_COUNT", F.lit(1))
     .withColumn("LOAD_TIMESTAMP", F.current_timestamp())
     .filter(F.col("MEME_KEY").isNotNull() & F.col("PLPL_KEY").isNotNull()
             & F.col("GRGR_KEY").isNotNull() & F.col("TXN_SRC_KEY").isNotNull()
             & F.col("COVERAGE_START_DATE_KEY").isNotNull())
)
fact.write.format("delta").mode("overwrite").option("overwriteSchema", "true").saveAsTable(f"{GOLD}.fact_enrollment")

The final .filter(...) enforces referential integrity at write time — a Gold row that fails to resolve against any required dimension (e.g. a plan code dimension row wasn't built yet) is excluded from the fact table rather than being written with a null foreign key.

docs.text: MedEnroll834 orchestrates its end-to-end workflow with Apache Airflow 3.x, running in Docker Compose with the CeleryExecutor. Airflow sits above the pipeline as pure orchestration — it owns scheduling, retries, task dependencies, and failure handling, but no transformation logic itself lives in a DAG task beyond thin calls into src/medenroll834/.
