  2. PYTHONPATH=/opt/airflow/project makes those imports resolve inside the Airflow container without a separate pip install -e . step at container build time.
  3. _PIP_ADDITIONAL_REQUIREMENTS installs databricks-sdk, boto3, and psycopg2-binary at container startup (the official Airflow image doesn't ship these by default).

docs.title: Configuration precedence
docs.text:
Every pipeline secret/setting can be overridden by an Airflow Variable, falling back to the environment variable if unset:

def _cfg(key: str, default: str | None = None) -> str | None:
    try:
        from airflow.models import Variable
        val = Variable.get(key, default_var=None)
        if val:
            return val
    except Exception:
        pass
    return os.environ.get(key, default)

This lets an operator override DATABRICKS_WAREHOUSE_ID or GENIE_SPACE_ID from the Airflow UI (Admin → Variables) without touching .env or restarting containers — useful for pointing at a different SQL warehouse during a one-off investigation.

docs.title: Why CeleryExecutor (not LocalExecutor)
docs.text:
CeleryExecutor was chosen over the simpler LocalExecutor so the airflow-worker service can scale independently of the scheduler — the stack is structured the same way a production Airflow deployment would be, even though this POC runs a single worker replica.

See Chapter 21 for the actual DAG, and Chapter 32 for standing the stack up locally.

docs.title: 21. Airflow DAG Implementation
docs.text:
Source: 05_orchestration/airflow/01_dags/med834_e2e_pipeline.py

med834_e2e_pipeline is written with Airflow's TaskFlow API (@dag/@task decorators), which keeps each stage as a typed Python function with explicit inputs/outputs instead of operator boilerplate.

docs.title: DAG declaration
docs.text:
@dag(
    dag_id="med834_e2e_pipeline",
    description="MedEnroll834 e2e: 834 -> blob storage -> UC Volume -> Databricks -> OLTP DB -> Report/Genie",
    default_args={"owner": "med834enrl", "retries": 1, "retry_delay": timedelta(minutes=3)},
    schedule="@daily",
    start_date=pendulum.datetime(2026, 1, 1, tz="UTC"),
    catchup=False,
    tags=["med834enrl", "e2e", "medallion", "blob-storage"],
)
def med834_e2e():
    ...

catchup=False means no backfill runs are scheduled for the gap between start_date and "now" — only the daily run going forward. Every task inherits retries=1 with a 3-minute delay from default_args.

docs.title: Task graph
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A["generate_834(synthetic 834 file)"] --> B["upload_to_blob(blob storage landing/834/)"]
    B --> C["push_to_uc_volume(Databricks UC Volume)"]
    C --> D["run_databricks_job(medallion + OLAP notebook)"]
    D --> E["load_oltp_database(Gold -> PostgreSQL)"]
    E --> F["generate_report(HTML -> blob storage)"]
    F --> G["ask_genie(optional NL questions)"]
    C --> H["archive_blob(all_success, scoped to this run's keys)"]
    E --> H
    B --> I["quarantine_failed_files(one_failed, scoped to this run's keys)"]
    C --> I
    D --> I
    E --> I

local = generate_834()
uploaded = upload_to_blob(local)          # returns exact blob keys, e.g.
                                           # ["landing/834/enrollment_...834"]
pushed = push_to_uc_volume(uploaded)      # pushes + returns the same keys
run_id = run_databricks_job(pushed)
summary = load_oltp_database(run_id)
report = generate_report(summary)
genie = ask_genie(report)

# archive_blob depends on the core chain's own outputs (pushed, summary),
# not on genie -- default all_success trigger rule means Airflow skips it
# automatically if push/Databricks/OLTP failed.
archive_blob(pushed) << summary

# quarantine_failed_files (trigger_rule="one_failed") is wired to the same
# core chain and fires if any of those tasks failed or were UPSTREAM_FAILED,
# moving this run's exact files to failed/834/ instead of landing/834/.
quarantine_failed_files(uploaded) << [pushed, run_id, summary]

uploaded/pushed carry the exact blob keys this run touched end to end via XCom -- push_to_uc_volume, archive_blob, and quarantine_failed_files all operate on that list directly rather than re-listing landing/834/, so a concurrent or straggling file from another run can never be mistakenly archived or quarantined alongside this run's files. See Chapter 23 for why this replaced an earlier trigger_rule="all_done" + re-list design that could archive a file Databricks had actually failed to process.

docs.title: Why files are staged into a Unity Catalog Volume
docs.text:
UC_VOLUME_PATH = "/Volumes/med834enrl/edi/landing/834"

Serverless Databricks Free Edition cannot read external buckets directly, so push_to_uc_volume downloads each file from blob storage and re-uploads it into the UC Volume via WorkspaceClient().files.upload() before the Databricks job runs:

@task
def push_to_uc_volume(keys: list[str]) -> list[str]:
    """Pushes only the exact keys this run uploaded (received as an
    argument, never a fresh blob_storage.list_landing_files() call) and
    passes that same key list through unchanged."""
    from databricks.sdk import WorkspaceClient
    from src.medenroll834.storage import blob_storage
    w = WorkspaceClient()
    w.files.create_directory(UC_VOLUME_PATH)
    for key in keys:
        name = key.split("/")[-1]
        local = f"/tmp/{name}"
        blob_storage.download_file(key, local)
        with open(local, "rb") as fh:
            w.files.upload(f"{UC_VOLUME_PATH}/{name}", fh, overwrite=True)
    return keys

This is a POC-specific hop — in the enterprise target architecture where the landing layer is AWS S3 directly, a Databricks job with an instance profile can read S3 natively and this staging task would be unnecessary.

docs.title: Running and waiting on the Databricks job
docs.text:
@task
def run_databricks_job(_pushed_keys: list[str]) -> int:
    from databricks.sdk import WorkspaceClient
    job_id = int(_cfg("DATABRICKS_JOB_ID"))
    run = WorkspaceClient().jobs.run_now_and_wait(job_id=job_id)
    state = run.state.result_state.value if run.state and run.state.result_state else "UNKNOWN"
    if state != "SUCCESS":
        raise RuntimeError(f"Databricks job failed: {state}")
    return run.run_id

run_now_and_wait() blocks the Airflow task until the Databricks job finishes, so Airflow's own retry mechanism covers both transient Databricks API failures and job-level failures — a non-SUCCESS result state is raised as a Python exception, which Airflow treats as a task failure subject to the DAG's retries=1.

docs.title: Archiving is scoped and success-gated; failures are quarantined, not archived
docs.text:
@task
def archive_blob(keys: list[str]) -> int:
    """No trigger_rule override -- default all_success means Airflow skips
    this task automatically if push_to_uc_volume, run_databricks_job, or
    load_oltp_database failed. Wired directly off those tasks' outputs
    (pushed, summary), not off the optional generate_report/ask_genie
    branch."""
    from src.medenroll834.storage import blob_storage
    for key in keys:
        blob_storage.archive_834(key)
    return len(keys)


@task(trigger_rule="one_failed")
def quarantine_failed_files(keys: list[str] | None) -> int:
    """Fires if any task in the core chain (push_to_uc_volume,
    run_databricks_job, load_oltp_database, or upload_to_blob itself)
    failed or was UPSTREAM_FAILED. Moves this run's exact files to
    failed/834/ instead of leaving them ambiguous in landing/834/ or
    archiving them as if they had succeeded."""
    keys = keys or []
    if not keys:
        return 0
    from src.medenroll834.storage import blob_storage
    for key in keys:
        blob_storage.archive_834(key, archive_prefix="failed/834/")
    return len(keys)

An earlier version used trigger_rule="all_done" on a single archive_blob task that re-listed landing/834/ from scratch — that let archiving run (and silently move files) even when run_databricks_job/load_oltp_database had failed, and it was not scoped to the files this run actually uploaded. The current design fixes both problems: archive_blob only runs on full core-chain success and only touches this run's exact keys (passed through via XCom from upload_to_blob), while quarantine_failed_files handles the failure path explicitly by relocating those same keys to failed/834/ rather than silently archiving or leaving them in landing/834/. See Chapter 23 for the full failure-handling rationale.

docs.title: Genie is skippable
docs.text:
@task
def ask_genie(_report_uri: str) -> dict:
    space_id = _cfg("GENIE_SPACE_ID")
    if not space_id:
        print("GENIE_SPACE_ID not set - skipping Genie step")
        return {"skipped": True}
    ...

docs.title: 22. Idempotency & Incremental Processing
docs.text: Every layer in MedEnroll834 is designed so re-running it with the same input produces the same result — a core requirement for a pipeline that Airflow may retry automatically.

docs.title: Delta layer idempotency: overwrite + natural grain
docs.text:
Bronze, Silver, and Gold all write with mode("overwrite"):

# Bronze
parsed.write.format("delta").mode("overwrite").option("mergeSchema", "true")...

# Gold
gold_df.write.format("delta").mode("overwrite").option("mergeSchema", "true")...

Because each run re-derives its output entirely from the current landing directory's files, re-running the pipeline against the same input files produces byte-for-byte the same Bronze/Silver/Gold content — there is no incremental merge logic to get out of sync. The one exception is quarantine, which appends (see below), because quarantine history is meant to accumulate across runs, not reflect only the latest run.

docs.title: Gold-level deduplication
docs.text:
.dropDuplicates(["file_name", "member_id"])

Guards against a malformed or re-sent 834 file producing duplicate HL blocks for the same member within one file — Gold's grain is (file_name, member_id), so duplicates collapse to one row regardless of how many times a Silver row for that member appeared.

docs.title: OLTP idempotency: natural-key upserts
docs.text:
The PostgreSQL loader's reference-entity inserts use ON CONFLICT ... DO UPDATE, keyed on each table's natural unique key:

cur.execute(
    "INSERT INTO core.core_grgr_group (grgr_num, st_cd, eff_dt, crtd_ts, updt_ts) "
    "VALUES (%s,%s,%s,%s,%s) ON CONFLICT (grgr_num) DO UPDATE SET updt_ts=EXCLUDED.updt_ts "
    "RETURNING grgr_id",
    ...
)
Table Natural key Upsert behavior core_grgr_group grgr_num Update updt_ts on conflict core_plpl_plan plpl_cd Update updt_ts on conflict core_mesb_subscriber sbsb_num Update updt_ts on conflict

Re-running load_gold_to_oltp() against the same Gold data therefore does not create duplicate groups, plans, or subscribers — only their updt_ts advances. (Member and enrollment rows are plain inserts in this simplified demo schema, not idempotent upserts — see Chapter 17 and Chapter 37 for the natural extension.)

docs.title: OLAP idempotency: deterministic hashed keys
docs.text: DIM_TRANSACTION_SOURCE.TXN_ID is derived with F.abs(F.xxhash64("file_name")) rather than an auto-incrementing counter — the same file name always produces the same TXN_ID across repeated notebook runs, so re-running the medallion job does not fork transaction-source identity for the same file.

docs.title: Transactional atomicity
docs.text:
Both the OLTP loader and the OLTP schema deployment script wrap all work in a single transaction:

conn.autocommit = False
try:
    ...  # all inserts/upserts
    conn.commit()
except Exception:
    conn.rollback()
    raise

A failure partway through either operation leaves the database exactly as it was before the attempt — no partial writes to reconcile manually.

docs.title: Incremental processing: Change Data Feed
docs.text:
Gold is written with delta.enableChangeDataFeed: "true":

layers:
  gold:
    options:
      delta.enableChangeDataFeed: "true"

This enables a future consumer to read only rows that changed since a given Delta table version (spark.read.format("delta").option("readChangeData", "true").option("startingVersion", N)) instead of re-scanning the whole table — the current OLTP loader and report generator both still do a full SELECT * against Gold, so CDF is provisioned but not yet exploited; see Chapter 37 for making the OLTP load CDF-incremental.

docs.title: File-level idempotency boundary
docs.text: The Airflow DAG's archive_blob task moves this run's exact processed files out of landing/834/ into archive/834/ only after the core processing chain (push -> Databricks -> OLTP) succeeds (default all_success trigger rule, wired directly to that chain's XCom outputs — see Chapter 23). This means a given 834 file is only ever re-processed if it is manually moved back into landing/ — the pipeline itself does not re-ingest archived files on a subsequent scheduled run, which is what keeps daily runs idempotent at the file level even though Bronze/Silver/Gold are always full overwrites of "whatever is currently in landing." If the core chain fails instead, quarantine_failed_files moves the same files to failed/834/ rather than archiving or re-listing landing/834/ from scratch.

docs.title: Airflow-level retries
docs.text:
Every task in med834_e2e_pipeline inherits a blanket retry policy from default_args:

DEFAULT_ARGS = {"owner": "med834enrl", "retries": 1, "retry_delay": timedelta(minutes=3)}

A single transient failure (a Databricks API hiccup, a momentary network blip to blob storage) is automatically retried once, 3 minutes later, before the task — and the whole DAG run — is marked failed.

docs.title: Explicit failure propagation from Databricks
docs.text:
run_databricks_job treats a non-SUCCESS Databricks job result as a hard Python exception, so Airflow's retry/alerting machinery applies uniformly to both "the API call failed" and "the job ran but produced a bad result":

@task
def run_databricks_job(_count: int) -> int:
    run = WorkspaceClient().jobs.run_now_and_wait(job_id=job_id)
    state = run.state.result_state.value if run.state and run.state.result_state else "UNKNOWN"
    if state != "SUCCESS":
        raise RuntimeError(f"Databricks job failed: {state}")
    return run.run_id

docs.title: Transactional rollback (OLTP)
docs.text:
The OLTP loader and schema deployment script both catch broadly and roll back on any exception, re-raising afterward so Airflow still sees the task as failed:

try:
    ...  # all inserts/upserts in one transaction
    conn.commit()
except Exception:
    conn.rollback()
    raise
finally:
    cur.close()
    conn.close()

This guarantees the OLTP database never ends up partially loaded — a retry of load_oltp_database after a rollback starts from the same pre-load state, re-running the (idempotent, see Chapter 22) upsert logic cleanly.

docs.title: Per-query error isolation in reporting
docs.text:
The HTML report generator does not let one failing analytics query take down the whole report — each REPORT_QUERIES entry is wrapped individually:

for title, sql in REPORT_QUERIES:
    try:
        cols, rows = _run_query(w, wid, sql)
        sections.append(_table_html(title, cols, rows))
    except Exception as exc:
        sections.append(f"<h2>{title}</h2><p style='color:red'>Error: {exc}</p>")

A broken query renders as a visible red error message inline in the generated HTML report instead of crashing the generate_report task and blocking the rest of the report's sections — a deliberate degrade-gracefully choice for an analytics/reporting path (as opposed to the OLTP load, which intentionally fails hard and rolls back, because operational data integrity matters more than reporting completeness).

docs.title: Operational failure handling: archive vs. quarantine
docs.text:
@task
def archive_blob(keys: list[str]) -> int:
    ...  # default all_success trigger rule

@task(trigger_rule="one_failed")
def quarantine_failed_files(keys: list[str] | None) -> int:
    ...

Unlike an earlier trigger_rule="all_done" design (which re-listed landing/834/ from scratch and could archive a file Databricks had actually failed to process), the archive/quarantine split is now both run-scoped and failure-aware:

  • archive_blob has the default all_success trigger rule and is wired directly to push_to_uc_volume/load_oltp_database's own XCom outputs (not to the optional generate_report/ask_genie branch), so Airflow automatically skips it if any task in the core processing chain failed — it is structurally impossible for it to archive a file that Databricks or the OLTP load never actually succeeded on.
  • quarantine_failed_files uses trigger_rule="one_failed" and is wired to every task in that same core chain (upload_to_blob, push_to_uc_volume, run_databricks_job, load_oltp_database). Airflow's ONE_FAILED rule fires whenever a direct upstream is FAILED or UPSTREAM_FAILED — confirmed against the Airflow 3.3.0 TriggerRuleDep source — so a failure anywhere in the chain reaches this task even if it only manifests several hops downstream as UPSTREAM_FAILED. It moves this run's exact files to failed/834/ instead of leaving them ambiguous in landing/834/.
  • Both tasks operate on the exact blob keys this run uploaded (upload_to_blob returns them, threaded unchanged through push_to_uc_volume via XCom) rather than re-listing the bucket, so a concurrent run's files are never touched by either path.
  • A missing/None keys XCom (e.g. upload_to_blob itself is what failed, so it never returned anything) is handled as a no-op in quarantine_failed_files, not an error — there is nothing to move.

The DAG run as a whole is still reported as failed if any upstream task failed; archive/quarantine only decide what happens to the landing files, not the DAG run's final state.

docs.title: Validation errors are not failures
docs.text: A critical distinction in this pipeline: a member record failing data-quality validation is not a pipeline failure — it is expected, handled output. is_valid=False rows are quarantined (see Chapter 16), not raised as exceptions; only infrastructure/connectivity/job-level problems trigger Airflow's retry and failure-reporting path.

docs.title: Known error classes and their handling
docs.text: Failure Where caught Behavior Databricks job non-SUCCESS run_databricks_job task RuntimeError → Airflow retry (1x) → DAG failure OLTP connection/constraint error load_gold_to_oltp() Transaction rollback → re-raise → Airflow retry Blob storage token expired/invalid any blob_storage.* call requests/boto3 exception → Airflow retry Single bad analytics SQL query generate_report() Caught per-query, rendered as an error row, report still completes Member record fails validation SilverLayer._apply_validation() Not an exception — routed to quarantine (see Ch. 16) Databricks SQL warehouse read failure _run_query() / _read_gold_from_databricks() RuntimeError with the Databricks error message, propagated up Core chain (push/Databricks/OLTP) failure quarantine_failed_files (trigger_rule="one_failed") This run's exact files moved to failed/834/; never archived

docs.title: 24. Observability
docs.text: MedEnroll834's observability is deliberately lightweight for a POC — structured, configurable logging with run-id correlation, pipeline-level run summaries, and Airflow's own task UI — rather than a separate metrics/tracing stack, but every signal that exists is real and wired into actual code paths.

docs.title: Standardized, configurable logging
docs.text:
Source: src/medenroll834/common/logging.py

def setup_logging(name: str = "med834enrl") -> logging.Logger:
    """Console handler always on; env-driven level + optional rotating file
    handler. Every record also gets run_id/file_name injected via a
    logging.Filter backed by a contextvar (see run_context() below)."""
    logger = logging.getLogger(name)
    if logger.handlers:
        return logger
    level = _resolve_level()  # MED834_LOG_LEVEL, default INFO
    logger.setLevel(level)
    formatter = logging.Formatter(LOG_FORMAT, datefmt=DATE_FORMAT)

    stream_handler = logging.StreamHandler(sys.stdout)
    stream_handler.setFormatter(formatter)
    stream_handler.addFilter(_CONTEXT_FILTER)
    logger.addHandler(stream_handler)

    if os.environ.get("MED834_LOG_FILE"):   # optional rotating file handler
        ...
    return logger

def log_pipeline_start(logger, layer: str, details: str) -> float:
    logger.info("START %s | %s | %s", layer, details, datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat())
    return time.monotonic()  # feed into log_pipeline_end/_error for duration

def log_pipeline_end(logger, layer: str, details: str, start_time=None) -> None:
    if start_time is not None:
        details = f"{details} | duration_s={time.monotonic() - start_time:.2f}"
    logger.info("END %s | %s | %s", layer, details, datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat())

def log_pipeline_error(logger, layer: str, details: str, start_time=None) -> None:
    """Call from an except block -- logs full traceback via logger.exception()."""
    ...

Env vars: MED834_LOG_LEVEL (default INFO), MED834_LOG_FILE (optional, adds a RotatingFileHandler alongside stdout), MED834_LOG_MAX_BYTES, MED834_LOG_BACKUP_COUNT. Wired into docker-compose.yaml for the Airflow containers and documented in .env.example.

Every layer (BronzeLayer, SilverLayer, GoldLayer, DeltaQuarantineManager, the OLTP loader, the report generator) calls log_pipeline_start/log_pipeline_end with a layer name and a details string that includes the actual row count and elapsed duration, e.g.:

2026-10-04 10:40:23 [INFO] bronze | run=3f9a21 file=- - START BRONZE | landing_path=10_data/raw/ | 2026-10-04T10:40:23+00:00
2026-10-04 10:40:25 [INFO] bronze | run=3f9a21 file=- - END BRONZE | files=2 segments_loaded=83 | duration_s=1.84 | 2026-10-04T10:40:25+00:00
2026-10-04 10:40:26 [INFO] silver | run=3f9a21 file=- - END SILVER | total=6 valid=6 invalid=0 | duration_s=0.92 | 2026-10-04T10:40:26+00:00
2026-10-04 10:40:27 [INFO] gold | run=3f9a21 file=- - END GOLD | records=6 | duration_s=0.41 | 2026-10-04T10:40:27+00:00

Logger names (bronze, silver, gold, quarantine, pipeline, validator, oltp_loader, report_generator, s3_utils, blob_storage, edi834_parser, airflow_dag) make it trivial to additionally grep/filter logs by component, and the logger.handlers guard in setup_logging() prevents duplicate log lines if it is called more than once for the same name within a process.

docs.title: Pipeline run-context correlation
docs.text:
run_context()/set_run_context() in common/logging.py

Every log line above carries run=3f9a21 — a contextvars.ContextVar bound once per pipeline invocation and injected into every LogRecord via a logging.Filter, so Bronze/Silver/Gold/Quarantine (each of which calls setup_logging() independently, since they are separate classes instantiated by the orchestrator) share one correlation id without threading run_id through every method signature:

# src/medenroll834/ingestion/pipeline.py
def run(self, landing_path: str, run_id: Optional[str] = None) -> Dict:
    run_id = run_id or uuid.uuid4().hex[:12]
    with run_context(run_id=run_id):
        ...  # every log line emitted by bronze/silver/gold/quarantine
             # during this `with` block carries run=<run_id>

The Airflow DAG does the same per-task, binding the Airflow dag_run.run_id (via get_current_context()["run_id"]) so a human can grep the Airflow task log and the pipeline module logs together for one DAG run, and forwards that same id to the Databricks job as a job_parameters={"airflow_run_id": ...} value — the notebook reads it back via dbutils.widgets.get("airflow_run_id") and includes it in its own print() lines, closing the loop from Airflow UI -> task log -> Databricks job run log.

docs.title: Error logging
docs.text: log_pipeline_error() is called from every layer's top-level except block before re-raising, so failures are never silently swallowed: it logs via logger.exception(), which captures the full traceback plus the elapsed duration up to the point of failure. Modules with no "layer" concept (s3_utils, blob_storage, oltp_loader's Databricks read, report_generator's Genie call) use logger.exception()/logger.error() directly at each external I/O call site (S3/blob upload-download-archive, SQL warehouse statement execution, Genie conversation) with the operation's key identifiers (bucket/key, warehouse_id, space_id) in the message -- credentials/tokens are never included.

docs.title: Pipeline-level run summaries
docs.text:
DeltaMedallionPipeline.run() returns a structured summary dict rather than just logging — this makes the pipeline's outcome programmatically consumable (by a test, by a future Airflow XCom, by a monitoring script):

summary = {
    "run_id": run_id,
    "bronze_segments": bronze_df.count(),
    "silver_total": silver_df.count(),
    "silver_valid": valid_df.count(),
    "silver_invalid": invalid_df.count(),
    "gold_records": gold_df.count(),
}

The Databricks notebook job produces an equivalent structured result and exits with it explicitly:

result["airflow_run_id"] = RUN_ID
print("MEDALLION RESULT:", json.dumps(result, indent=2))
dbutils.notebook.exit(json.dumps(result))

dbutils.notebook.exit() makes this result retrievable from the Databricks Jobs API by anything that calls the job (including the Airflow task), without needing to parse log output.

docs.title: Airflow-native observability
docs.text:
• Task graph UI (localhost:8080) shows per-task state (queued/running/success/failed/retried) for every DAG run.
  • Per-task logs are captured automatically by Airflow and viewable per task instance; the DAG's own tasks use logging.getLogger-based loggers (not bare print()) so their output is level-tagged and run-id-tagged consistently with the pipeline's own setup_logging() output, which still appears within the same task log.
  • DAG import error detection: airflow dags list-import-errors — used as a CI-style sanity check (07_scripts/03_utils/validate_dag.py) before deploying a DAG change.

docs.title: OLTP and OLAP lineage columns
docs.text:
Both stores carry lineage back to the originating 834 file:

  • OLTP: every core_meen_enrollment row FKs to an enrl_edxn_transaction.txn_id, which stores file_nm, rcvd_ts, and proc_stat.
  • OLAP: DIM_TRANSACTION_SOURCE.FILE_NAME + FACT_ENROLLMENT.TXN_SRC_KEY trace every fact row back to its source file.
  • Delta: file_name is carried as a column through Bronze → Silver → Gold → quarantine, so any row can be traced to its source file without a separate lineage table.

docs.title: What's deliberately out of scope for this POC
docs.text: No Prometheus/Grafana metrics stack, no distributed tracing (OpenTelemetry), and no alerting integration are wired up for this POC. See Chapter 37 for the monitoring roadmap.

docs.title: 25. Spark Performance Optimization
docs.text: Every Spark tuning decision documented here is an actual configuration or code change in this repo, most captured with an inline comment explaining the real failure it fixed — not generic Spark tuning advice.

docs.title: Adaptive Query Execution (AQE)
docs.text:
.config("spark.sql.adaptive.enabled", "true")
.config("spark.sql.adaptive.coalescePartitions.enabled", "true")
.config("spark.sql.shuffle.partitions", "8")

AQE lets Spark re-plan shuffle partition counts at runtime based on actual data size rather than a fixed guess, and coalescePartitions merges small post-shuffle partitions automatically — important for this pipeline's small-to-medium local/POC data volumes where a fixed large partition count would create excessive task overhead. shuffle.partitions=8 is tuned down from Spark's default of 200, appropriate for local/local[*] execution rather than a large cluster.

docs.title: Broadcast map instead of a self-join (biggest algorithmic win)
docs.text:
The single largest performance/correctness fix in the codebase: resolving each dependent's subscriber via hl_parent_id/hl_id was originally a self-join, which fanned out catastrophically because HL ids repeat across transaction sets (see Chapter 14):

# Implemented with a broadcast map rather than a self-join. A join here
# duplicated every dependent against every candidate subscriber and
# blew the executor heap; a broadcast lookup is O(1) per row and cannot
# fan out because the key set is collapsed with first().
subscriber_map = {
    f"{r['hl_key']}|{r['hl_id']}": r["member_id"]
    for r in base.filter(F.col("is_subscriber"))
    .select("hl_key", "hl_id", "member_id")
    .dropDuplicates(["hl_key", "hl_id"])
    .collect()
}

Collecting only the (small) distinct-subscriber set and broadcasting it as a Spark create_map() expression turns an O(n²)-shaped join into an O(1) per-row map lookup — this scales with the number of subscribers, not the number of members, which is the correct scaling dimension for this workload.

docs.title: Window-based "carry forward latest value" instead of a loop
docs.text:
file_order = Window.partitionBy("file_name").orderBy(F.col("seg_row"))
ordered = ordered.withColumn(
    "txn_row",
    F.last(F.when(F.col("segment_id") == "ST", F.col("seg_row")), ignorenulls=True)
     .over(file_order.rowsBetween(Window.unboundedPreceding, Window.currentRow)),
)

A previous version range-joined every segment against every ST row to find "the most recent transaction start," which matched a segment against all preceding transaction sets and multiplied member rows roughly 5x. A cumulative-window last(..., ignorenulls=True) carries the most recent value forward in a single pass with no join at all.

docs.title: Delta write-time optimization
docs.text:
# Bronze
.option("delta.autoOptimize.optimizeWrite", "true")

Compacts small files at write time — relevant because 834 ingestion produces many small per-segment row batches per file; without optimizeWrite, Bronze would accumulate a large number of tiny Parquet files under the Delta table over many pipeline runs, degrading future read performance.

docs.title: Delta retention tuning
docs.text:
silver:
  options:
    delta.deletedFileRetentionDuration: "interval 7 days"

Keeps a 7-day time-travel window on Silver for debugging/auditing without retaining deleted files indefinitely (the Delta default is 30 days via VACUUM's retention check) — a deliberate storage-cost vs. debuggability tradeoff for this layer specifically.

docs.title: Change Data Feed for future incremental reads
docs.text:
gold:
  options:
    delta.enableChangeDataFeed: "true"

Enabled proactively so a future consumer can read only changed rows since a given version instead of a full re-scan — see Chapter 22 for the current state (not yet exploited by the OLTP loader) and Chapter 37 for the roadmap.

docs.title: Databricks-side: read_files() + explode() over a Python loop
docs.text:
The Databricks notebook job reads landing files with a single distributed-SQL statement rather than iterating files in Python, because it must scale across a cluster reading many files from a Unity Catalog Volume at once (see Chapter 13):

raw = spark.sql(
    f"SELECT value, element_at(split(_metadata.file_path, '/'), -1) AS file_name "
    f"FROM read_files('{LANDING}', format => 'text', wholeText => true)"
)
bronze = raw.withColumn("segment", F.explode(F.split(F.regexp_replace("value", r"[\r\n]+", "~"), "~"))) ...

monotonically_increasing_id() is used for seg_order in this distributed path (rather than a Python enumerate()), since it can be computed without collecting data back to the driver.

docs.title: 26. Benchmark Framework
docs.text:
What exists vs. what is proposed

This repository does not currently ship a dedicated, automated benchmark harness (e.g. a script that runs N file sizes and plots throughput). What exists is the instrumentation a benchmark framework would consume — pipeline run summaries, per-layer logging, and a validated smoke-test baseline. This chapter documents that real instrumentation, then proposes a concrete framework design that is not yet implemented. See Chapter 34 for the actual measured numbers vs. the legacy design targets.

docs.title: What already exists to build a benchmark on
1. Structured per-run summaries
docs.text:
DeltaMedallionPipeline.run() returns row counts for every layer on every run:

summary = {
    "bronze_segments": bronze_df.count(),
    "silver_total": silver_df.count(),
    "silver_valid": valid_df.count(),
    "silver_invalid": invalid_df.count(),
    "gold_records": gold_df.count(),
}

This is already a timed, structured artifact — wrapping the call in time.perf_counter() before/after gives per-run wall-clock duration for free, with no change to pipeline code.

docs.title: 2. Timestamped layer-boundary logs
docs.text:
log_pipeline_start/log_pipeline_end emit ISO-8601 timestamps at the start and end of every layer (Bronze, Silver, Gold, Quarantine):

START BRONZE | landing_path=10_data/raw/ | 2026-10-04T10:40:23+00:00
END BRONZE   | segments_loaded=83        | 2026-10-04T10:40:25+00:00

Parsing these gives per-layer duration breakdowns (Bronze vs. Silver vs. Gold time), which is more actionable than a single end-to-end number when deciding where to optimize.

docs.title: 3. A known, reproducible smoke-test baseline
docs.text:
BRONZE     : segments_loaded = 83
SILVER     : total = 6, valid = 6, invalid = 0
GOLD       : records = 6
QUARANTINE : records = 0

(1 synthetic file, 3 subscribers + 3 dependents — see PIPELINE_STATUS.md). This is a real, run result, suitable as a regression baseline: any future change that alters these counts for the same input is a signal worth investigating.

docs.title: Proposed framework design (not yet implemented)
docs.text:
A natural next step, using only what's already in the repo:

# proposed: 07_scripts/03_utils/benchmark_pipeline.py
import time
from generator.synthetic_834_generator import generate_batch
from src.medenroll834.ingestion.pipeline import DeltaMedallionPipeline
from src.medenroll834.common.spark_session import get_local_spark

SIZES = [(1, 10), (5, 100), (10, 1000), (20, 5000)]  # (files, subscribers_per_file)

def run_benchmark():
    spark = get_local_spark("benchmark")
    results = []
    for num_files, subs in SIZES:
        generate_batch("10_data/bench_raw", num_files=num_files, subscribers_per_file=subs)
        pipeline = DeltaMedallionPipeline(spark)
        start = time.perf_counter()
        summary = pipeline.run("10_data/bench_raw")
        elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start
        results.append({"files": num_files, "subs": subs, "elapsed_s": elapsed, **summary})
    return results

This would reuse generate_batch() (Chapter 10) and DeltaMedallionPipeline (Chapter 18) exactly as-is — no pipeline code changes needed, only a new orchestrating script that scales input size and records elapsed time per run.

docs.text:
Dimension Metric Source Volume Records/sec at increasing file sizes summary["gold_records"] / elapsed_s Velocity End-to-end wall-clock time per run time.perf_counter() around pipeline.run() Variety Validation pass rate as plan-code/field variety increases silver_valid / silver_total Reliability Quarantine rate under --messy synthetic data silver_invalid / silver_total

See Chapter 34 for how these dimensions map back to the legacy system's documented constraints.

docs.title: 27. Databricks SQL Dashboard
docs.text:
Source: src/medenroll834/reporting/report_generator.py

Rather than a separate BI tool, MedEnroll834's analytics layer runs a fixed set of SQL queries against Databricks SQL warehouses and renders them as a single self-contained HTML report — a deliberately simple "traditional analytics" consumption path that pairs with Genie's "AI analytics" path (see Chapter 4).

docs.title: The seven report queries
docs.text:
REPORT_QUERIES: List[Tuple[str, str]] = [
    ("Total enrollments", "SELECT COUNT(*) AS total FROM med834enrl.edi.gold_enrollments"),
    ("Members by plan",
     "SELECT plan_id, COUNT(*) AS members FROM med834enrl.edi.gold_enrollments "
     "GROUP BY plan_id ORDER BY members DESC"),
    ("Members by state",
     "SELECT state, COUNT(*) AS members FROM med834enrl.edi.gold_enrollments "
     "WHERE state IS NOT NULL GROUP BY state ORDER BY members DESC LIMIT 15"),
    ("Subscriber vs dependent",
     "SELECT is_subscriber, COUNT(*) AS members FROM med834enrl.edi.gold_enrollments "
     "GROUP BY is_subscriber"),
    ("Average age by plan",
     "SELECT plan_id, ROUND(AVG(age_years),1) AS avg_age FROM med834enrl.edi.gold_enrollments "
     "GROUP BY plan_id ORDER BY avg_age DESC"),
    ("Enrollments by plan (FACT_ENROLLMENT star schema)",
     "SELECT p.PLAN_CODE, COUNT(*) AS enrollments "
     "FROM med834enrl.gold.FACT_ENROLLMENT f "
     "JOIN med834enrl.gold.DIM_PLAN p ON f.PLPL_KEY = p.PLPL_KEY "
     "GROUP BY p.PLAN_CODE ORDER BY enrollments DESC"),
    ("Enrollments by group and plan (FACT_ENROLLMENT star schema)",
     "SELECT gr.GROUP_NUMBER, p.PLAN_CODE, COUNT(*) AS enrollments "
     "FROM med834enrl.gold.FACT_ENROLLMENT f "
     "JOIN med834enrl.gold.DIM_GROUP gr ON f.GRGR_KEY = gr.GRGR_KEY "
     "JOIN med834enrl.gold.DIM_PLAN p ON f.PLPL_KEY = p.PLPL_KEY "
     "GROUP BY gr.GROUP_NUMBER, p.PLAN_CODE ORDER BY enrollments DESC LIMIT 15"),
]

Notice the first five queries hit the flat gold_enrollments table directly, while the last two join through the OLAP star schema (FACT_ENROLLMENT + DIM_PLAN/DIM_GROUP) — demonstrating both consumption shapes from the same analytics entry point.

docs.title: Executing against a SQL warehouse
docs.text:
def _run_query(w, warehouse_id, sql):
    from databricks.sdk.service.sql import StatementState
    resp = w.statement_execution.execute_statement(
        warehouse_id=warehouse_id, statement=sql, wait_timeout="50s"
    )
    while resp.status.state in (StatementState.PENDING, StatementState.RUNNING):
        time.sleep(2)
        resp = w.statement_execution.get_statement(resp.statement_id)
    if resp.status.state != StatementState.SUCCEEDED:
        raise RuntimeError(f"Query failed: {resp.status.error.message}")
    return [c.name for c in resp.manifest.schema.columns], resp.result.data_array or []

Uses the Databricks SQL Statement Execution API — the serverless warehouse spins up on demand if not already running, with a 2-second poll loop while PENDING/RUNNING.

docs.title: Rendering self-contained HTML
docs.text:
def generate_report(profile=None, warehouse_id=None) -> str:
    w = _client(profile)
    wid = _warehouse_id(w, warehouse_id)
    sections = []
    for title, sql in REPORT_QUERIES:
        try:
            cols, rows = _run_query(w, wid, sql)
            sections.append(_table_html(title, cols, rows))
        except Exception as exc:
            sections.append(f"<h2>{title}</h2><p style='color:red'>Error: {exc}</p>")
    return (
        "<!DOCTYPE html><html>...<title>MedEnroll834 Enrollment Report</title>..."
        f"<p>Generated: {generated} | Source: med834enrl.edi.gold_enrollments</p>"
        + "".join(sections) + "</body></html>"
    )

The report is a single HTML string with inline CSS — no external dependencies, no JavaScript — so it can be written straight to blob storage (audit/reports/enrollment_report_<timestamp>.html) and opened in any browser with no server required. Each query's failure is isolated (see Chapter 23), so one broken query renders a red error message inline rather than failing the whole report.

docs.title: 28. Genie / GenAI
docs.text:
Source: src/medenroll834/reporting/report_generator.py (ask_genie())

Databricks Genie is the pipeline's natural-language analytics consumer — the second of the two analytical consumption modes described in Chapter 4. It queries the exact same governed Gold/OLAP tables as the HTML report; it is not a different data source and not a pipeline transformation step.

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text:
def ask_genie(space_id: str, question: str, profile=None) -> Dict:
    """Ask a Databricks Genie space a natural-language question.

    Requires a Genie space (space_id) in a workspace with Genie enabled.
    Returns the final message payload. Best-effort: raises if Genie API or
    space is unavailable.
    """
    w = _client(profile)
    conv = w.genie.start_conversation_and_wait(space_id=space_id, content=question)
    out = {"question": question, "attachments": []}
    for att in (conv.attachments or []):
        if att.text:
            out["attachments"].append({"type": "text", "content": att.text.content})
        if att.query:
            out["attachments"].append({"type": "query", "query": att.query.query,
                                        "description": att.query.description})
    return out

start_conversation_and_wait() blocks until Genie has processed the question and returns, synchronously, a list of attachments — each either a natural-language text answer or a generated SQL query (with description) that Genie ran to produce that answer. Surfacing the generated SQL alongside the text answer is valuable for auditability: a reviewer can see exactly what query Genie executed against the governed Gold/OLAP data, not just trust an opaque answer.

docs.title: Invoked from the Airflow DAG (optional)
docs.text:
@task
def ask_genie(_report_uri: str) -> dict:
    space_id = _cfg("GENIE_SPACE_ID")
    if not space_id:
        print("GENIE_SPACE_ID not set - skipping Genie step")
        return {"skipped": True}
    from src.medenroll834.reporting.report_generator import ask_genie as genie
    qs = ["How many members are enrolled on each plan?",
          "What is the subscriber to dependent ratio?"]
    answers = [genie(space_id, q) for q in qs]
    return {"answers": answers}

Two representative questions are asked on every DAG run when GENIE_SPACE_ID is configured — chosen because they mirror two of the HTML report's own queries ("Members by plan", "Subscriber vs dependent"), demonstrating that the NL path and the fixed-SQL path answer the same underlying business questions through different interfaces.

docs.title: Enabling Genie
docs.text:
From the E2E Pipeline Runbook:

  1. In Databricks: Genie → New space, add med834enrl.edi.gold_enrollments and med834enrl.gold.* tables as the space's data.
  2. Copy the space id from the URL and set GENIE_SPACE_ID in .env.
  3. Re-run the DAG; ask_genie now queries the same governed Gold/OLAP data as the HTML report.

docs.title: Why Genie is optional, not required
docs.text: GENIE_SPACE_ID is intentionally unset by default — the pipeline runs fully end-to-end (generation → ingestion → medallion → OLTP → HTML report → archive) with Genie entirely skipped. This reflects its position as an additional analytical consumption mode layered on top of a complete, independently-functioning pipeline, not a required dependency of it.

docs.title: Positioning note (why this matters architecturally)
docs.text:
A common modernization-story mistake is to treat an AI/NL feature as part of the data pipeline's transformation logic. This repo deliberately keeps Genie downstream of Gold/OLAP, alongside — not inside — the HTML reporting path, so:

  • Pipeline reliability (Bronze/Silver/Gold/OLTP) never depends on Genie's availability.
  • Both consumption modes are governed by the same data quality rules applied upstream (see Chapter 16) — Genie cannot "see" data that never passed validation.
  • Swapping or removing Genie has zero blast radius on the rest of the system — see Chapter 4 for the architectural framing this reflects.

docs.text:
Source: 04_infrastructure/01_terraform/s3_pipeline_least_privilege_policy.json

{
  "Statement": [
    { "Sid": "ListTheBucket", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "s3:ListBucket",

docs.title: Database connection security
docs.text: OLTP_DATABASE_URL requires ?sslmode=require for the managed Postgres provider used in this POC — enforced by convention/documentation (see the PostgreSQL Setup chapter) rather than programmatically, since psycopg2.connect() accepts the sslmode as part of the connection string itself.

docs.title: Transactional integrity as a security property
docs.text: Both the OLTP schema deployment and the OLTP data load wrap all statements in a single transaction with rollback on any exception (see Chapter 23) — this prevents a failed deploy or load from leaving the database in a state where constraints/FKs are partially applied, which could otherwise be an integrity/availability risk.

docs.title: PHI/PII posture
docs.text:
This project processes zero production member data — every 834 file is synthetically generated (see Chapter 10). That said, the schema and pipeline are structured as if the data were real PHI/PII, per SECURITY.md:

  • Compliance with HIPAA regulations is a stated design goal for any production deployment of this architecture.
  • Data encryption at rest (S3 SSE, Delta/Parquet on encrypted storage) and in transit (sslmode=require, HTTPS-only S3 policy) are both already enforced at the infrastructure level documented above.
  • Access logging/auditing is intentionally left as a future improvement — out of scope for this POC's synthetic-data threat model.

docs.title: CI pipeline (ci.yml)
docs.text:
Triggered on every push/PR to main or develop, with three parallel jobs:

flowchart LR
    T["push / pull_request(main, develop)"] --> L["lintruff + mypy + black --check"]
    T --> TEST["testpytest (3.10, 3.11 matrix)"]
    T --> SEC["securitybandit + safety"]
    TEST --> COV["codecov upload"]

jobs:
  lint:
    steps:
      - run: pip install -r requirements.txt
      - run: ruff check src/ 02_tests/
      - run: mypy src/
      - run: black --check src/ 02_tests/

  test:
    strategy:
      matrix:
        python-version: ['3.10', '3.11']
    steps:
      - run: pytest 02_tests/ -v --cov=src --cov-report=xml --cov-report=term-missing
      - uses: codecov/codecov-action@v3

  security:
    steps:
      - run: pip install bandit safety
      - run: bandit -r src/ -f json -o bandit-report.json
      - run: safety check --json > safety-report.json
  • lint — ruff (fast linter), mypy (static typing), black --check (formatting, no auto-fix in CI).
  • test — runs across a Python 3.10 / 3.11 matrix, uploads coverage to Codecov.
  • security — bandit (static security scan of src/) and safety (dependency vulnerability check) — see Chapter 29.

lint and test both reference src/ and 02_tests/, matching pyproject.toml's testpaths = ["02_tests"] and the Makefile's own pytest 02_tests/ -v target exactly — an earlier version of this workflow referenced a non-existent tests/ directory, which meant CI would not actually find or run the test suite; that mismatch has been fixed.

docs.text:
Triggered only on version tags (v*):

flowchart LR
    TAG["push tag v*"] --> BUILD["buildpython -m build -> dist/"]
    BUILD --> DOCKER["dockerbuildx + push to DockerHub"]
    DOCKER --> DEPLOY["deployproduction environment"]

jobs:
  build:
    steps:
      - run: pip install build twine
      - run: python -m build
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v3
        with: { name: dist, path: dist/ }

  docker:
    needs: build
    steps:
      - uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}
          password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}
      - uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
        with: { context: ., push: true, tags: ..., labels: ... }

  deploy:
    needs: [build, docker]
    environment: production
    steps:
      - run: echo "Deployment steps would go here"

The deploy job is a documented placeholder — it runs in a GitHub Environment named production (so it can be gated with required reviewers/approval rules in repo settings) but the actual deployment command (kubectl apply / helm upgrade) is intentionally commented out, since this POC has no Kubernetes/Helm target yet.

docs.title: 34. Legacy vs Modern Benchmark
docs.text:
Measured vs. design target

This chapter clearly separates numbers actually measured in this repository from the legacy system's documented constraint, which was never independently re-measured against the new pipeline at equivalent scale. Presenting one as the other would be misleading — see Chapter 26 for how to close this gap with real throughput testing.

docs.title: Legacy system (documented constraint)
docs.text:
Source: Chapter 2, business-problem framing.

Enrollment processing jobs in the legacy system are observed to take approximately one hour end to end for a full daily batch file, across the full EDI → ECA → Legacy Programs → SCP → CORE Programs chain. This number describes the existing production workflow's behavior as reported by the business, not a benchmark run against this repository's code.

docs.title: Modern pipeline (measured, smoke-test scale)
docs.text:
Source: PIPELINE_STATUS.md, "VERIFIED: End-to-End Run" section.

A real, reproducible run of this repository's DeltaMedallionPipeline against 1 synthetic file (3 subscribers + 3 dependents) produced:

BRONZE     : segments_loaded = 83
SILVER     : total = 6, valid = 6, invalid = 0
GOLD       : records = 6
QUARANTINE : records = 0

All four Delta tables were written with a valid _delta_log. This confirms functional correctness end to end (parsing, HL resolution, validation, dedup, Delta writes) — it is not yet a throughput/scale measurement at anything near the legacy system's full daily batch volume.

docs.title: Qualitative comparison (architecturally grounded)
docs.text: Dimension Legacy Modern (this repo) Processing model Serial, single-machine, 6+ distinct tools (EDI/ECA/Legacy Programs/SCP/Bash/CORE Programs) Distributed PySpark/Delta, 3-layer medallion (see Ch. 13–18) Parallelism None — one file processed at a time, one machine Spark partitions data across cores/executors automatically (AQE, see Ch. 25) Failure isolation A failure in any of 6 tools (EDI/ECA/Legacy Programs/SCP/Bash/CORE Programs) stops the chain with separate logs per tool Per-layer logging with structured log_pipeline_start/end (see Ch. 24); invalid records (not whole files) are quarantined, not fatal (see Ch. 16) Recoverability Manual investigation across 6 tool logs Idempotent re-runs (see Ch. 22); Airflow automatic retry (see Ch. 23) Analytical access None — CORE System keyword-file load only OLAP star schema + Databricks SQL + Genie (see Ch. 19, Ch. 27–28) Data lineage Proprietary intermediate format, no shared trace file_name carried through every layer; ENRL_EDXN_TRANSACTION/DIM_TRANSACTION_SOURCE FK every record to its source file Observability 6 separate tool-specific logs Unified structured logging + per-run summary dicts (see Ch. 24) Infrastructure as Code Manually configured Tidal/SSIS/DataStage jobs Terraform (S3), SQL DDL scripts, Docker Compose, all version-controlled

docs.title: What a rigorous head-to-head benchmark would require
docs.text:
1. Generate synthetic 834 data at a representative daily-batch scale using generate_batch() with a large subscribers_per_file.
  2. Run DeltaMedallionPipeline.run() against it on a representative Databricks cluster size, timed with the methodology proposed in Chapter 26.
  3. Compare wall-clock time directly against the legacy system's ~1 hour figure, at the same record count.

This has not yet been executed in this repository — the honest claim this documentation makes is about architecture (distributed vs. serial, quarantine vs. hard-fail, governed analytics vs. none), not a measured speedup multiplier.

docs.title: Velocity
docs.text: The legacy chain's six-tool handoff (EDI → ECA → Legacy Programs → SCP → Bash → CORE Programs, see Chapter 3) means enrollment changes are only as fast as the slowest, most fragile link in that chain. The modern pipeline collapses this into a single orchestrated DAG (med834_e2e_pipeline) with Airflow-managed retries, reducing the number of places a delay or failure can silently accumulate. Faster, more predictable enrollment processing means coverage is active sooner — which matters directly to members submitting claims against a plan that hasn't finished loading yet.

docs.title: Volume
docs.text: Distributed PySpark processing (see Chapter 25) scales horizontally with file/record count, rather than being bound to a single machine's throughput ceiling the way the legacy chain is. The business impact is a pipeline whose capacity grows with the Databricks cluster/warehouse size provisioned, not with the age and specs of a specific on-prem server.

docs.title: Variety
docs.text: A single validation ruleset (DataFrameValidator, Chapter 16) applied consistently across every record — rather than variety handling being spread implicitly across 6 different tools' individual quirks — means a new plan code, relationship type, or malformed field is caught and explained (validation_errors) in one place, by one team, instead of surfacing as an opaque downstream CORE System load failure.

docs.title: Operational cost reduction
docs.text:
• Fewer tools to license, patch, and staff — Tidal, SSIS, DataStage, Legacy Programs, SCP, and Bash scripts are five-to-six separate operational surfaces; the modern stack is Airflow + Databricks + PostgreSQL.
  • Unified observability reduces mean-time-to-diagnosis: a structured log line (START SILVER | ...) and a per-run summary dict (silver_invalid=12) replace grepping six different tool-specific log formats (see Chapter 24).
  • Idempotent re-runs (see Chapter 22) mean a failed run can simply be retried rather than requiring manual reconciliation of partial state.

docs.title: New analytical capability (not present in the legacy system at all)
docs.text:
The legacy flow terminates at a CORE System keyword-file load — there is no historical reporting, BI, or ad hoc analytics path. The modern platform adds, at no cost to the operational path:

  • An OLAP star schema (FACT_ENROLLMENT + 5 dimensions, Chapter 19) purpose-built for enrollment analytics.
  • A traditional analytics path: scheduled HTML reports over fixed KPIs (Chapter 27).
  • An AI analytics path: natural-language ad hoc exploration via Genie (Chapter 28), answering questions like "How many members are enrolled on each plan?" without writing SQL.

This is a genuinely new business capability, not a modernization of an existing one — the legacy architecture has no equivalent to show stakeholders a trend in enrollment-by-plan over time, for example.

docs.title: Compliance and audit posture
docs.text: Every enrollment record and every rejected record traces back to its source file via a transaction identifier (ENRL_EDXN_TRANSACTION/DIM_TRANSACTION_SOURCE, see Chapter 24) — a stronger audit trail than the legacy proprietary intermediate format allows, which matters directly for HIPAA-adjacent compliance reviews (see Chapter 29).

docs.title: MedEnroll834 — Modern Distributed Data Platform for Growing Data
docs.text: A proof-of-concept healthcare data platform that demonstrates how distributed processing modernizes HIPAA X12 834 enrollment transaction processing — built to show the same architectural pattern (distributed processing + OLTP/OLAP separation + BI/AI consumption) generalizes beyond this one business module.

docs.title: Highlights
docs.text:
• Distributed medallion pipeline (Bronze → Silver → Gold) in PySpark 4.0+ / Delta Lake, parsing real X12 834 (5010) EDI structure including the HL hierarchy, segment extraction, and date normalization.
  • Dual persistence: PostgreSQL OLTP for operational reads/writes, a Delta Lake star schema (FACT_ENROLLMENT + 5 dimensions) for analytics — deliberately kept architecturally separate.
  • Dual analytics consumption: a traditional SQL/HTML reporting path and a Databricks Genie natural-language AI path, both querying the same governed Gold/OLAP data.
  • Apache Airflow 3.x orchestration (TaskFlow API, CeleryExecutor) with retries, run-scoped archive-on-success / quarantine-on-failure handling, and Airflow Variable config overrides.
  • Data quality by design: Spark-SQL validation rules producing multi-reason error arrays, with invalid records quarantined (not dropped) to a dedicated Delta table.
  • Idempotent throughout: Delta overwrite semantics, PostgreSQL natural-key upserts, deterministic hashed surrogate keys.
  • Infrastructure as Code: Terraform-managed S3 bucket + least-privilege IAM policy, versioned SQL DDL for both OLTP and OLAP schemas, full Docker Compose local dev stack.
  • CI/CD: GitHub Actions — lint (ruff/mypy/black), test (pytest matrix, Codecov), security scan (bandit/safety), build/Docker publish on tag.
  • Zero production data: all 834 files are synthetically generated with a custom X12-compliant generator (realistic name/address/plan pools, valid ISA checksums).

docs.title: 37. Future Improvements
docs.text: A concrete, prioritized roadmap grounded in gaps and TODOs actually identified while building this documentation — not a generic wishlist.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
• Extend coverage to oltp_loader.py and report_generator.py — both currently require a live Databricks workspace and PostgreSQL instance to exercise (see Chapter 30). Mocking databricks.sdk.WorkspaceClient and psycopg2.connect would let these modules run in CI without live infrastructure.
  • Add a true end-to-end Airflow task-execution test — current DAG validation (validate_dag.py) only checks import/parse correctness, not that tasks actually execute correctly against mocked dependencies.
  • Add --messy synthetic data test cases so the quarantine path (Chapter 16) has automated test coverage, not just manual verification.

docs.title: Performance & benchmarking
docs.text:
• Implement the benchmark framework proposed in Chapter 26 — scale synthetic data generation across a range of file/record counts and measure actual wall-clock throughput, to get a real number against the legacy system's documented ~1 hour per batch constraint (see Chapter 34).

  • Exploit Delta Change Data Feed for incremental OLTP loads — gold is already written with delta.enableChangeDataFeed: "true", but load_gold_to_oltp() still does a full SELECT * against Gold on every run. Switching to readChangeData/startingVersion would make repeated OLTP loads proportional to what changed, not the full table size.

docs.title: Data model
docs.text:
• Make core_meme_member / core_meen_enrollment upsertable — these are currently plain inserts (see Chapter 17), unlike the natural-key-upserted group/plan/subscriber tables. A natural key (e.g. mesb_id + rltn_cd + eff_dt) would let member/enrollment loads be fully idempotent rather than relying on upstream Gold deduplication alone.
  • Add SCD Type 2 history tracking to the OLTP schema, mirroring the CURRENT_FLAG pattern already used in the OLAP dimensions (Chapter 9), so an OLTP member's historical plan changes are queryable, not just the current state.

docs.title: Observability
docs.text:
• Add a 09_monitoring/ metrics/alerting stack (e.g. Prometheus + Grafana, or a lightweight Airflow-native alerting integration) — none currently exists (see Chapter 24).
  • Add structured JSON logging (vs. the current human-readable-formatted log lines) so logs can be ingested by a log aggregation platform without custom parsing.
  • Add access/audit logging for PHI/PII-adjacent operations, per the compliance posture discussed in Chapter 29 — not yet implemented since this POC processes only synthetic data.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
• Complete the AWS S3 migration described in Chapter 7 and Chapter 33 — swap upload_to_blob/archive_blob DAG tasks for the already-built src/medenroll834/s3/s3_utils.py equivalents, eliminating the POC's blob-storage-to-UC-Volume staging hop entirely (a Databricks job with an instance profile can read S3 directly).
  • Generalize the parser to other X12 transaction types (837 claims, 270/271 eligibility) to validate the "reusable platform" claim made in Chapter 1 beyond the 834 module alone.
  • CD pipeline's deploy job is currently a documented placeholder (see Chapter 31) — wiring an actual Kubernetes/Helm (or Databricks Asset Bundle) deployment target would complete the CI/CD story end to end.
